sens: Exotic four-legged animal with thick fur, imported from Africa or Asia in antiquity
Creature brought as loot or object of wealth and prestige
H8500.detail: 1. The monkey is an exotic animal, likely originating from Africa or Asia, characterized by its fur-covered body and four limbs. In the two parallel passages of 1 Kings 10:22 and 2 Chronicles 9:21, monkeys are listed among the rare and precious goods that the ships of Tarshish bring every three years to King Solomon: gold, silver, ivory, monkeys, and peacocks. These exotic animals, unknown or very rare in Israel, represent prestigious acquisitions, symbols of the king's wealth and power.
H8500.origine: The Hebrew word תֻּכִּיִּים (toukkim) likely refers to a species of primate. Its precise etymology remains uncertain, but it may have roots in ancient Semitic or Indo-Iranian languages, reflecting distant trade contacts with Africa and Asia. The word appears only in lists of royal wealth, suggesting a borrowing from foreign languages to name an animal unknown in the Promised Land.
H8500.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible: in the two parallel accounts of Solomon's wealth (1 Kings 10:22 and 2 Chronicles 9:21). In these two passages, monkeys are listed as exotic goods brought by the king's merchant fleets every three years, alongside gold, silver, ivory, and peacocks. They symbolize international commercial power and Solomon's royal prestige at the height of his reign. The term carries no particular metaphorical or symbolic charge: it simply denotes a rare and distant commodity.
H8500.portee: For the reader, monkeys remind us that Solomon's wealth came from his wisdom, which allowed him to establish distant trade routes and import unknown treasures. This example invites recognition that the most prestigious goods often come from trust in God and the wise use of one's intelligence. However, the same enumeration of riches serves as a backdrop to the vanity that Solomon will later denounce in Ecclesiastes, showing that exotic treasures do not satisfy the heart.

sens: State of complete and flawless accomplishment
Limit, end, term of a thing
Character of absence of lack or restriction
H8502.detail:
1. Perfection refers to the state of something that has reached its complete accomplishment, without any flaw or lack. It is the realized totality, the fulfillment of what was promised or expected. In Psalms 119:96, the psalmist observes that even 'perfect' things — that is, the commandments of men or human creations that seem complete — have 'bounds,' a limit that shows their finitude.
2. By extension, perfection implies a limit or an end: it is the point where a progression stops, where something has nothing more to add. The word thus evokes the idea of a closed totality, an accomplishment without remainder.
3. On a more abstract level, it is the absence of lack or restriction. God's commandments, unlike limited human works, have 'no limit' — they possess a perfection that does not confine but opens to infinity.
H8502.origine: The Hebrew word תִּכְלָה comes from the root כ-ל-ה which means 'to finish,' 'to accomplish,' 'to complete.' This same root gives rise to words in the family of 'complete' and 'fulfillment.' The basic idea is that of an action reaching its end, of a totality being fulfilled. In the Greek Old Testament, words like τέλειος ('perfect') share this notion of accomplishment and fullness.
H8502.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 119:96. The context is that of Psalm 119, a long hymn to divine commandments that celebrates the Law. The psalmist meditates on the nature of God's commandments and compares them to human achievements. He recognizes that everything that comes from men — even what they consider 'perfect' — carries within it natural limits, boundaries that mark its relative incompleteness. In contrast, the Word of God transcends these bounds. It is in comparison with this finite human perfection that the infinity of the divine Word shines.
H8502.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that human perfection, even at its best, remains limited and relative. Only the Word and commandments of God possess an unlimited perfection. This invites us not to place our trust in the works or wisdom of the world, but to discover in the divine Law a wisdom of another dimension — infinite, eternal, complete.

sens: State of completion or fullness
Limit or boundary of a space
Extreme point or end of a thing
H8503.detail:
1. The primary idea is that of a complete realization, without flaw or lack — a total accomplishment. When the Psalmist speaks of a 'perfect hatred' towards God's enemies (Psalms 139:22), he means a total, entire hatred, without compromise or reservation. This perfection is a fullness.
2. The word also denotes a boundary or limit that marks where something ends. Job 26:10 uses it to delineate the 'boundary' between light and darkness — the line that separates two areas. It is the end of a domain.
3. By extension, it is the place where something stops: Job 28:3 speaks of the 'places' deepest in the earth, meaning the extreme points where human search goes. Similarly, in Nehemiah 3:21, the 'extremity' of the house is its end, its last point.
H8503.origine: The word comes from a root that means 'to complete,' 'to finish,' 'to bring to term.' It evokes the idea of bringing something to its final point, to where it can go no further. This root is found in other Hebrew words related to end and accomplishment. The basic image is that of something complete because it extends to its natural end.
H8503.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible. Job uses it mainly in dialogues about the limits of human knowledge: one cannot 'reach perfect knowledge' of God (Job 11:7), and man can explore only up to a certain 'limit' (Job 26:10). In Nehemiah 3:21 and Job 28:3, it denotes the physical extremity of a place. Psalm 139:22 uses it to express the integrity of a feeling: a 'perfect' hatred, without hesitation. The word circulates between the idea of completion (what is fully realized) and that of boundary (what marks a limit).
H8503.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on their own limits: I cannot know God in His totality, there are boundaries to my understanding. But it also speaks of the possibility of complete dedication — a perfect hatred of evil, an obedience without reservation. It is an opportunity to ask God for sincerity and complete integrity in faith.

sens: Blue or violet color obtained by dyeing
Thread or wool dyed blue
Fabric or cloth dyed blue
Colored material used for priestly garments and the furnishings of the sanctuary
H8504.detail:
1. Blue is a color obtained by dyeing, probably from a shellfish or a plant — it is a precious and sought-after dye. Exodus 25:4 requests "blue dyed fabrics" as raw material for constructing the tabernacle.
2. The term "blue thread" is also used when referring to the thread itself, before it is woven: Exodus 28:8 mentions "blue thread" for the belt of the high priest's ephod.
3. The fabric or cloth dyed blue constitutes a valuable material: Exodus 39:1 recounts that sacred garments were made "with blue dyed fabrics."
4. In worship, blue carries a sacred meaning: it is a color reserved for the ornaments of the sanctuary and the garments of the priests, mixed with purple and crimson. Numbers 15:38 makes it a distinctive mark of God's covenant with Israel.
H8504.origine: The word comes from a root that denotes the act of dyeing or coloring. It appears mainly in descriptions of the tabernacle and priestly garments, where it is always accompanied by purple and crimson. It is a color of prestige in antiquity, difficult to obtain and therefore costly, which explains why it adorns the garments of worship and sacred objects.
H8504.emploi: The word appears 49 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the books that describe the tabernacle and its ornaments (Exodus, Numbers, 2 Chronicles). It designates the blue in the sacred garments of Aaron — the ephod, the robe, the urim and thummim — and in the veil of the tabernacle. It also appears when listing the materials brought as offerings (Exodus 35:25, where the women of Israel spin blue thread). Finally, it is seen in later texts, such as Esther 1:6, where blue adorns the king's court, or Ezekiel 23:6, where it symbolizes luxury and seduction. Thus, it is both a liturgical color and a sign of wealth.
H8504.portee: Blue reminds the reader that the worship of the true God requires beauty and order: it is not a religion of poverty or neglect, but of excellence offered to God. The recurrence of blue — always mixed with purple and crimson — emphasizes that the worshiper must come with their best. For Israel, blue was also a sign of holy identity, marking the difference between the chosen people and the surrounding nations.

sens: Determine the weight or mass of something with a scale or measuring instrument
Evaluate, estimate the value or importance of something
Examine, probe thoughts, intentions, or hearts
Establish, set, or adjust something according to a measure or standard
Be in balance, be just or right
H8505.detail:
1. The primary meaning is concrete: to weigh something on a scale to know its mass. This is the basic image of the word: an object is placed on one side of the scale, and weights are added on the other until balance is achieved. In 1 Samuel 2:3, God "weighs" all the actions of men, as on a divine scale.

2. From there, the word takes on a broader meaning: to evaluate, estimate, consider carefully. It involves judging the value or importance of something. This is characteristic of Him who, in Proverbs 16:2 and 24:12, "weighs the spirits" and "weighs the hearts" — He examines and judges them internally.

3. The word can also mean to probe, scrutinize: in Isaiah 40:13, no one has "measured" the Spirit of the Lord, meaning that no creature can explore or measure the depth of His wisdom.

4. In a context of construction or order, the word means to fix, establish, adjust: in Job 28:25, God "fixed" the measure of the waters, establishing their limit and quantity precisely.

5. The word can finally carry the idea of being right, just, equal: in Ezekiel 18:29, God asks if His way is not "right" — that is, fair, in balance, without leaning to one side or the other.
H8505.origine: The Hebrew verb תָּכַן (takan) comes from a root that expresses the fundamental idea of balance, measure, and regularity. The word evokes the action of placing something in balance, weighing it on a scale, and then, by extension, evaluating, judging, adjusting. In Hebrew, words from the same family all convey this notion of measure, adjustment, and rectitude. The verb expresses the action of one who brings order, who adjusts according to an established standard.
H8505.emploi: This verb appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom and prophetic books. In 1 Samuel 2:3, God "weighs" human actions — it is a divine activity of judgment. In Proverbs (16:2, 21:2, 24:12), the word regularly describes how God "weighs" or scrutinizes hearts, hidden intentions, contrary to deceptive appearances. In Isaiah 40:12-13, the cosmic context: God has "fixed" the dimensions of the universe (waters, wind, dust), demonstrating His absolute mastery. In Ezekiel (18:25, 18:29, 33:17-20), the word carries the idea of justice and righteousness: is God's way "right"? The people contest whether divine judgments are just. The meaning varies according to the context: the act of weighing (concrete), moral evaluation (judgment of hearts), or affirmation of divine justice (righteousness).
H8505.portee: This word reveals that God does not judge by appearances: He "weighs" our hearts, scrutinizes our most secret intentions, far beyond what we show the world. It invites the believer to recognize that nothing escapes the penetrating gaze of the Father, and that true justice comes from One who knows absolutely. It is a source of respectful fear before divine wisdom, but also of trust: God judges with perfect precision, equitable as a perfectly balanced scale.

sens: What is measured, evaluated as a fixed portion
A determined measure, a reference standard
What must be produced or delivered according to a standard
H8506.detail:
1. The word first designates a measured portion, something that can be counted or weighed. In Exodus 5:18, the Hebrews must produce a fixed quantity of bricks each day, despite the shortage of straw: it is an imposed burden, precisely calculated.
2. It is also a standard, an official measure to which one refers. In Ezekiel 45:11, the ephah (measure of grain) and the bath (measure of liquid) must have "the same measure": each is worth one-tenth of a homer, it is a regulation of equivalence.
3. By extension, the word can designate the quantity that is required or that must be achieved, the standard to be respected. It sets the limit, stating "you must produce this and no less."
H8506.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to fix, determine, establish." It is from the same family as other Hebrew words related to order, arrangement, or what is established according to a rule. The underlying image is that of something stable, precisely fixed, that cannot be exceeded or arbitrarily diminished.
H8506.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 5:18, it designates the daily quantity of bricks that the Hebrew workers must produce: it is a hard quota to reach, even in impossible circumstances (without raw materials). In Ezekiel 45:11, it appears in a vision of the restored temple, where God establishes the exact measurements of containers and portions. Both uses share the idea of a precise, imperative standard that allows no deviation.
H8506.portee: This word reminds the reader that God establishes just and precise rules, but also that human standards (here the brick quota) can be overwhelming and unjust. In Ezekiel, it expresses divine order and wisdom: God organizes all things with accuracy. For the Christian, it is an opportunity to see how the Bible speaks of both human oppression and divine rectitude.

sens: City in the territory of Simeon during the time of David
H8507.detail: Thoken is a city that the sons of Simeon possessed until the time of King David. It is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:32 in a list of five cities of the tribe of Simeon (Etham, Ain, Rimmon, Thoken, and Aschan), indicating its role as a center of habitation and probably as an administrative or residential base for this tribe.
H8507.origine: The Hebrew name Tochen literally means "measure" or what is "measured." This meaning suggests that the city may have been named for its role as a place of measurement, market, or evaluation of goods, a common practice in urban centers of antiquity.
H8507.emploi: Thoken appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:32, in the context of the lands allotted to the tribe of Simeon. This unique mention highlights the importance of documenting the cities and territories of the tribes of Israel during the Davidic period, even though most of these localities are otherwise very little known to us.

sens: Measure or proportion of a thing, its regular dimension
Plan or model of a construction, in its proportions and details
Beauty or completion in form, visible perfection
H8508.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the exact measure of a thing, the harmonious proportion of its parts: it is the idea of architecture or creation that adheres to precise rules. In Ezekiel 43:10, the prophet invites Israel to contemplate "the plan" of the restored temple, that is, its measured structure and exact proportions.
2. Therefore, the word can also mean the model or the plan itself, the drawing used for construction. Ezekiel 43:10 speaks of the "plan" of the temple that the people must measure and study, like an architect following the outlines of a construction.
3. In Ezekiel 28:12, applied to the king of Tyre, the word takes on a more figurative hue: "You were the seal of perfection" means that this king was the accomplished model, the finished figure of beauty and wisdom. It is perfection as a harmonious totality, as completeness without flaw.
H8508.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to measure" or "to draw lines." It is related to the idea of proportion, of a just relationship between parts. The same root produces words designating practical wisdom or the art of building with balance. It is a concrete word: it paints the image of a regular outline, a measure that divides and orders space.
H8508.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in Ezekiel, the prophet of architectural visions. In Ezekiel 43:10, it denotes the measured proportions of the future temple, an object of contemplation and repentance for Israel. In Ezekiel 28:12, the same word qualifies the king of Tyre, no longer as a material construction but as a creature made in perfect model: it is the only application of the word to a person in all of Scripture. This rarity underscores its weight: Ezekiel uses it to evoke the divine order, visible in sacred architecture as well as in the original beauty of the creature.
H8508.portee: This word reminds us that God creates and builds according to a wisdom of proportions and harmony. For the Christian, contemplating the plan of the temple or the beauty of a creature is to glimpse the order and perfection of the divine design. It also invites humility: the visible perfection in creation, whether architectural or personal, is never more than a reflection of that which comes from God.

sens: Luxurious long garment that covers the body
Insignia of dignity and official honor
H8509.detail:
1. The mantle is a loose, long garment that covers a large part of the body. In the only passage where it appears, that of Esther 8:15, it is made of fine linen and dyed purple — precious materials reserved for high-ranking individuals. It is a garment of display, not a simple everyday garment.
2. This type of mantle was not only functional: it marked social status and authority. When Mordecai wears it in Esther 8:15, it is the visible sign that the king has clothed him with honor and elevated him to a position of power. The mantle proclaims to the world the change in Mordecai's fate, from a condemned prisoner to the king's advisor.
H8509.origine: The Hebrew word belongs to the family of terms designating prestige garments in the ancient East. Its root evokes the idea of wrapping or covering. In biblical Hebrew, various words distinguish garments according to their function or fabric; this one specifically applies to a garment of display, a mark of royal or princely status. The fine linen mentioned here — fine thread from Egyptian flax — reinforces this dimension of extraordinary luxury.
H8509.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Esther 8:15. In this decisive moment of the narrative, after Mordecai has been saved from the death sentence and elevated to honors, the mantle becomes the external symbol of his new dignity. It is associated with other royal insignia: the golden crown and the blue and white colors of the king. This context shows that the mantle does not designate a simple garment, but a display that publicly signals a change of authority and prestige. The crowds of Susa who see Mordecai leave the palace with this mantle immediately recognize his elevation.
H8509.portee: This word reminds us that in the biblical narrative, God can suddenly reverse destinies. Mordecai, threatened with death, leaves the royal palace wrapped in visible glory — a concrete image of the deliverance and honor that God grants to those who remain faithful to Him. For the reader, the royal mantle teaches that true dignity comes from God and is recognized even by the powerful of the world.

sens: Heap of debris from a destroyed city
Hill or elevation on which a city was built
Archaeological vestige, accumulation of ancient debris
H8510.detail:
1. The word denotes the accumulation of stone, earth, and debris that remains after a city has been burned and razed. It is the dismal sight of complete destruction: collapsed walls, houses reduced to ashes, all reduced to a shapeless heap. In Deuteronomy 13:16 and Joshua 8:28, the cities of Ai and the one that sinned against God become heaps of ruins, never to be rebuilt — a permanent monument to ruin.
2. The word also designates the hill, the topographical elevation itself on which the ancient city stood. In Joshua 11:13, the cities "situated on hills" escape the fire, except for Hazor. It is the physical form of the land, the relief.
3. In Jeremiah, the word evokes the ruins of a past city, the tangible remains of a once-prosperous habitation. In Jeremiah 30:18, the city "will be rebuilt on its ruins": it is the site of an ancient city, now a field of debris, that is being restored.
H8510.origine: The Hebrew word תֵּל (tel) fundamentally means a mound or a heap. It is related to the idea of accumulation, of piling up. In biblical archaeology, a "tell" is precisely the artificially formed hill created by the superposition of ruins of ancient cities — each destruction, each reconstruction layered creates this distinctive shape. The Hebrew word captures this reality of the ancient Levant: cities were rebuilt on their own ruins, progressively creating distinctive mounds.
H8510.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible. Deuteronomy 13:16 and Joshua 8:28 use it to describe the definitive destruction of a city: it becomes a heap of ruins, a permanent warning. Joshua 11:13 uses it to designate the hill itself, the geographical elevation. Jeremiah 30:18 and 49:2 speak of destruction and restoration: a ravaged city is nothing but ruins, upon which one can rebuild. The context oscillates between the idea of destruction (heap of debris) and that of a geographical place (hill, urban site).
H8510.portee: This word reminds us that God's judgments on sin are real and visible. Cities become heaps of ruins — not by accident, but by divine discipline. But Jeremiah also shows that even upon the ruins, God can rebuild and restore His people: ruin is not the end. The Christian can meditate on the consequence of sin and on the mercy that raises the ruins.

sens: To hold something in the air, attached to a fixed point, without it resting on the ground
To be attached to something, to remain stuck to it
To lean towards something, to be inclined to, drawn towards
H8511.detail:
1. Suspend means to hold something in the air, fixed to a point above, without it touching the ground. This is the most direct physical image: in 2 Samuel 21:12, the Philistines hung the bodies of Saul and Jonathan at Beth-Shean, meaning they left them hanging as a public spectacle.
2. The word can also mean to remain stuck to something, to be attached or glued to it. This is an image of dependence or physical clinginess.
3. Figuratively, to suspend means to lean towards something, to be inclined to, naturally drawn in a direction. In Hosea 11:7, the people of Israel are "inclined" to stray from God — they lean, they tend towards this separation as if naturally. In Deuteronomy 28:66, life is like "suspended," tossed about, unstable, hanging by a fragile thread.
H8511.origine: The Hebrew root תלא (tala) primarily evokes the action of holding, hanging, remaining suspended. It paints the image of something that hangs, floats, that depends on a support point. The word belongs to the common vocabulary of movement and positioning verbs in Hebrew. It is a concrete image that quickly enriches itself with figurative meanings: what hangs risks falling, what is suspended is fragile, uncertain; one who leans towards something is naturally inclined to it.
H8511.emploi: The verb תלא appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first used in a literal and concrete sense in 2 Samuel 21:12: hanging corpses is an act of desecration and humiliation towards the dead. It then takes on an existential and anxious meaning in Deuteronomy 28:66, where the life of the unfaithful people will be like suspended, uncertain, fragile — a threat of curse. Finally, in Hosea 11:7, it shifts towards the figurative sense of inclination, natural tendency: the people lean, incline towards abandoning God, while God calls them back. The meaning progresses from the concrete (physically hanging) to the psychological and moral (leaning in heart, being drawn towards).
H8511.portee: This word helps to grasp two important truths. First, the fragility of life without God: in Deuteronomy, it is like a thread, exposed at every moment to breaking. Secondly, the danger of moral inclination: when one leans towards evil, one gradually distances oneself from God. Hosea reminds us that this inclination to sin does not chain us — God "calls us back to the Most High" — a call to repentance and return.

sens: City of Babylon located on the river Chebar
H8512.detail: Tel-Aviv is a city of ancient Babylon where the prophet Ezekiel was deported and where he received his prophetic visions. The name literally means "hill of the flood" or "mound of ruin" in Hebrew, evoking the remnants of an ancient city. It is on the banks of the river Chebar, probably a branch of the Euphrates, that Ezekiel settled among the exiles of Judah (Ezekiel 3:15).
H8512.origine: The Hebrew name תֵּל אָבִיב (Tel Aviv) is composed of two words: תֵּל (tel) meaning "hill" or "mound" — an artificial hill formed by the overlapping ruins of ancient cities — and אָבִיב (abib) which means "spring" or "green harvest," but also "flood" or "ruin." This formation of geographical names is typical of the ancient Near East, where archaeologists still identify ancient sites by these characteristic mounds.
H8512.emploi: Tel-Aviv appears only once in the biblical text, in Ezekiel 3:15, in the account of Ezekiel's prophetic calling. This prophet was exiled there with the Judeans deported by King Nebuchadnezzar after the fall of Jerusalem, and it is in this city that God gave him his missions and visions. The context clearly indicates that Tel-Aviv is one of the colonies of Judean exiles established in Mesopotamia, alongside the river Chebar.

sens: Pain, physical or moral fatigue experienced in effort or trial
Suffering, felt pain
Distress, deep difficulty of the situation
Moral weariness, disgust in the face of a burden
Tribulations, trials endured over time
H8513.detail:
1. The word first designates the fatigue that accompanies a painful effort, the pain of labor: Moses tells Jethro "all the sufferings that had befallen them on the way" during the exodus (Exodus 18:8), meaning the pains and trials of the journey.
2. It can also express physical pain, the suffering felt within: the psalmist says that God "has surrounded me with poison and pain" (Lamentations 3:5), evoking a suffering that besieges him.
3. The word characterizes the distress of a difficult situation: in Numbers 20:14, Moses speaks of "all the sufferings we have experienced," meaning the totality of the tribulations and trials the people have gone through.
4. It can also express moral exhaustion and disgust: in Malachi 1:13, the priests complain "What a weariness!" before the divine service, revealing a spiritual weariness that drives them to contempt.
5. In a broader perspective, the word encompasses all tribulations, the accumulated pains: Nehemiah asks God not to regard as little "all the sufferings" of the people throughout the centuries (Nehemiah 9:32).
H8513.origine: The Hebrew word תְּלָאָה (telâah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of fatigue and exhausting work. It belongs to a family of words expressing effort, weariness, and exhaustion. The image is that of a suffering endured, a burden weighing on the one who bears it, whether physical or moral.
H8513.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Old Testament, concentrated in historical and prophetic narratives. It first describes the trials of the people at the exit from Egypt (Exodus 18:8), then their subsequent tribulations (Numbers 20:14, Nehemiah 9:32). The word can express immediate, personal, and intimate suffering (Lamentations 3:5), or moral weariness in the face of the demands of divine service (Malachi 1:13). Its uses thus blend physical fatigue, pain, historical distress, and spiritual disgust, showing that this term captures all aspects of human suffering, from the most concrete to the deepest.
H8513.portee: This word reminds every reader that the life of God's people, and ours, will not be free from suffering and fatigue. It invites the believer to recognize these trials as real and legitimate, not to ignore them. It also calls to seek in God the one who sees these sufferings, bears witness to them, and can transform them: suffering is not abandoned by God, it can be entrusted to His mercy.

sens: State of a dry land, without rain or moisture
Condition of extreme dryness that renders the land barren
H8514.detail:
1. Aridity refers to completely dry land, without water or rain: it is a desert where nothing grows. In Hosea 13:5, God says to Israel: "I knew you in the wilderness, in a dry land" — He speaks of Sinai, that inhospitable place where the people walked for forty years without water, depending solely on God to live.
2. Figuratively, aridity evokes trial, abandonment, suffering: a condition where one is deprived of what sustains life, where one must rely solely on God.
H8514.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of drying up, losing all moisture. It paints the image of land that has received no rain, where grass and crops die for lack of water. It is a concrete word that describes one of the greatest threats to a pastoral and agricultural people in the Middle East.
H8514.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Hosea 13:5. There it designates the desert of Sinai where God guided Israel after Egypt. God reminds His people that He knew and supported them in this arid place, deprived of natural resources — which underscores the extraordinary divine protection they benefited from. The context of Hosea is one of admonition: God reproaches Israel for having forgotten His faithfulness in the desert and for having worshiped idols once established in the fertile land of Canaan.
H8514.portee: This word reminds the believer of moments of spiritual dryness and trial, and how God remains present in them. Like Israel in the arid desert, we are sometimes placed in conditions where our own strength is insufficient, and where we must rely entirely on God. It is an invitation to trust and recognize His past faithfulness.

sens: City or region of Mesopotamia conquered by the Assyrians
Urban center in Assyrian territory
Place whose inhabitants had local gods
H8515.detail: Telassar is a city or region located in Mesopotamia, within the lands controlled by Assyria. It is part of the cities that the Assyrian king Sargon II (or his successor) had conquered and brought under his authority. Its name literally means "Assyrian hill" or "mound of Assyria." In the two passages where it is mentioned (2 Kings 19:12 and Isaiah 37:12), Telassar appears in a list of cities whose gods could not protect the inhabitants from Assyrian domination: Gozan, Haran, Retseph, and the sons of Eden. The king of Assyria mentions it to demonstrate his power: no local god has resisted his conquests.
H8515.origine: The Hebrew name תְּלַאשָּׂ֑ר (Telassar) literally means "Assyrian hill" or "Assyrian mound" (tel = hill, Assar = Assyria). This toponymy reflects the strategic and administrative importance of the place in Assyrian geography. It is the proper name of an ancient city, likely in the region of Upper Mesopotamia.
H8515.emploi: Telassar appears only twice in the Bible, in two nearly identical parallel passages (2 Kings 19:12 and Isaiah 37:12). In both cases, it is mentioned in the intimidating speech of an Assyrian officer addressed to King Hezekiah of Judah. This officer lists the cities that Assyria has conquered, along with their gods, to show that no one can resist Assyrian power — not even the gods of the defeated nations. Thus, Telassar is situated in a context of military propaganda and challenge to the faith of Israel.
H8515.portee: Telassar reminds the reader that even powerful civilizations and organized religions can be defeated by a superior military force. It also symbolizes the misplaced confidence that people place in their own strength and in false gods. For the people of Judah threatened by Assyria, Telassar must have been a terrifying name — but the faith of the prophet Isaiah and the deliverance of Jerusalem (narrated just afterward) show that the God of Israel is far above any Assyrian power.

sens: garment or piece of clothing that one wears
that which covers and protects the body
figuratively: that which one is clothed with morally or spiritually
H8516.detail:
1. The word refers to a garment, an article of clothing that one wears to cover oneself. It is a general term for anything that dresses the body.
2. In the literal sense, clothing envelops and protects: it is what one puts on oneself. In the vision of Isaiah 59:17, God "puts on righteousness like a breastplate" and "takes vengeance for clothing," using the image of clothing to describe what one wraps oneself in.
3. In a figurative and spiritual sense, clothing becomes that which covers internally: a quality, an attitude, a moral or divine reality. To be clothed with a garment means to be covered by it, to be filled with it. Isaiah uses it to express that God is clothed with His own attributes as one puts on clothing.
H8516.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to clothe" or "to put on." It expresses the idea of covering oneself, of putting something on. This root belongs to the same family as other Hebrew words related to clothing and the action of covering. The basic image is that of something one puts on, that one wears on the body for protection or presentation.
H8516.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 59:17. In this prophetic verse, the prophet employs the poetic image of clothing to describe how God arms Himself with His divine attributes: righteousness, salvation, vengeance, jealousy. By placing these spiritual realities in the metaphor of clothing one puts on, Isaiah expresses that these qualities are as real and active for God as clothing is for a warrior preparing for battle. It is highly figurative language, characteristic of prophetic poetry, that makes visible and tangible the invisible action of God.
H8516.portee: This passage shows how the Bible speaks of the invisible reality using material images that we know. Learning this word invites the reader to meditate on how God "clothes Himself" with His own perfections: He is righteous, He saves, He judges. It also reminds us that our own moral and spiritual qualities can be described as that which we are clothed with — we are called to "put on" Christ, love, humility.

sens: Ice crystals that fall from the sky and cover the earth
Immaculate whiteness, shining purity
H8517.detail:
1. Snow is the well-known meteorological phenomenon: frozen water that falls from the sky in the form of white crystals. It is a natural element that renders everything white and pure. In Daniel 7:9, the prophet sees the Ancient of Days clothed in a garment "white as snow" to evoke His majesty and absolute holiness.
2. The word is also used figuratively to signify moral and spiritual purity, spotless whiteness. When something is said to be "white as snow," it means that it is perfectly pure and without defect, which corresponds to the holiness of God in this vision.
H8517.origine: The Aramaic word תְּלַג (telag) comes from the same root as the Hebrew שֶׁלֶג (sheleg), which also means "snow." It is an ancient word that simply describes this natural phenomenon. In the Greek Old Testament, this Hebrew root regularly appears to express not only the meteorological fact but also the theological idea of divine purity.
H8517.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 7:9, in the major vision of the prophet Daniel. It is at this moment that the prophet contemplates the throne of God and describes the Ancient of Days with a garment white as snow. This unique context underscores the importance of the motif: the whiteness of snow symbolizes the transcendent holiness and brilliance of divinity. The context is not anecdotal but theological and apocalyptic.
H8517.portee: This image of snow illuminates what the Bible says about the holiness of God: it is absolute, radiant, without a trace of corruption. For the believer, it also reminds us that once forgiven, our crimson sins become white as snow (Isaiah 1:18). It is a promise of transformation and purity restored by grace.

sens: To fix something by suspending it at a point of attachment
To execute by hanging with a rope
To remain suspended in the air
To place or arrange in suspension for display or decoration
H8518.detail:
1. To hang primarily means to fix something by suspending it at a high point: shields hung on David's tower as war ornaments (Song of Solomon 4:4), or a body hanging from a tree after execution (Joshua 10:26).
2. To hang also means to execute someone by strangulation while suspending them: Pharaoh had the chief cupbearer hanged (Genesis 40:19), and Haman was hanged on the gallows he had prepared for another (Esther 7:10).
3. To be hanged means to remain suspended in the air: Absalom, fleeing on a mule, got caught by his hair in the branches of an oak (2 Samuel 18:10).
4. To suspend can also mean to place or expose something in a visible and intentional manner, either for decoration or as a public spectacle: the corpses of enemies were left hanging on the gallows as a warning (Deuteronomy 21:22-23).
H8518.origine: The Hebrew verb תָּלָה comes from a root that evokes the image of suspending, of holding something in balance above the void. The word is related to the idea of depending on something, of remaining attached. In Hebrew, the same root appears in derivatives that maintain the image of what hangs or rises.
H8518.emploi: The verb תָּלָה is used 26 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives. It frequently appears in Genesis and Deuteronomy to speak of execution by hanging (Genesis 40:19; Deuteronomy 21:22-23), where it is linked to the notion of curse. The book of Esther uses it several times to recount the hanging of Haman and his sons (Esther 7:9-10; 9:14). It is also found in poetic imagery: shields suspended on David's tower, or the sky hanging on nothing in Job (Job 26:7). The context thus shifts from judicial punishment to poetic imagery, but the underlying image remains: something that hangs suspended above the void.
H8518.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that in the Old Testament, hanging was a form of extreme misfortune, a visible curse (Deuteronomy 21:23). This image later illuminates the reading of the New Testament: Christ 'hanging' on the wood of the cross takes and transforms this curse into salvation. Understanding the weight of the Hebrew image helps to grasp why the cross could appear as a curse to those who saw it, and how salvation operates through it nonetheless.

sens: A complaint expressed in a low voice or in a whisper
Protest against authority or against a decision
Collective discontent of a group
Critical words directed against God
H8519.detail:
1. The murmur is primarily a complaint expressed discreetly, almost in a whisper, rather than an open cry. It is a word that circulates, from mouth to mouth, carried by discontent. In the desert, the Israelites 'murmur' against Moses and against God (Exodus 16:7-8).
2. It is also a direct protest against those in authority. The Israelites accuse Moses and Aaron of leading them to death in the desert. God hears these complaints and takes them seriously (Exodus 16:8-9).
3. The murmur becomes a collective act: the whole assembly murmurs, sharing the same doubt and concern. It is a sign of a people wavering in their trust (Numbers 14:27).
4. Ultimately, every murmur against human authority reveals a hidden rebellion against God Himself. God responds: it is not your murmurs against Moses that I hear, it is your lack of faith in me (Exodus 16:8).
H8519.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of complaint or protest. The same root produces the verb 'to murmur', of which the murmur is the fruit: it is the action of murmuring turned into a word, a sound of persistent discontent. This type of speech characterizes moments of crisis and collective doubt in the life of the people.
H8519.emploi: The word appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in two major episodes: the complaints in the desert after the exodus from Egypt (Exodus 16) and the rebellion of Korah (Numbers 14 and 17). In each case, God does not turn a deaf ear to the murmurs: He hears them, judges them, and responds. The murmur is never a detail; it is a form of rebellion that provokes God's anger and calls for His punishment or correction (Numbers 17:5, where God promises to 'put an end to the murmurs').
H8519.portee: For the believer reading these texts, the murmur becomes an internal alarm signal. It is the moment when fear replaces trust, when doubt spreads within the group. The Bible teaches us that God hears every complaint against His governance of the world, every veiled protest against His wisdom. The remedy is not forced silence, but the renewal of faith and acceptance of His will, even when it seems harsh.

sens: Man of the tribe of Ephraim during the divided monarchy
H8520.detail: Thelach is a man of the tribe of Ephraim mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of Ephraim. He is the son of Resheph and the father of Tachan (1 Chronicles 7:25). This name appears in a list of descendants that establishes family continuity within the tribe of Ephraim.
H8520.origine: The name Thelach means 'vigor' or 'strength' in Hebrew. It belongs to the tradition of Hebrew family names that evoked qualities or states. The name appears exclusively in the context of the priestly and tribal genealogies of the Old Testament.
H8520.emploi: Thelach is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:25, in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Ephraim. He occupies an intermediate position in this family line, which shows the importance given by the author of the book of Chronicles to the complete documentation of tribal genealogies after the exile.

sens: Location in Babylon mentioned in the lists of return from exile
Place of origin of families whose genealogy could not be established
H8521.detail: Thel-Harscha is a city in Babylon (modern-day Iraq), likely located in the lowlands near the sea. The name literally means 'mound of the deaf mute' in Hebrew. It appears only in the lists of those who returned from Babylonian captivity after Cyrus's decree: in Ezra 2:59, it is mentioned alongside Thel-Melah and Kerub-Addan as a city from which families could not prove their Israelite ancestry. This same list also appears in Nehemiah 7:61, confirming the administrative importance of this locality in recording the exiles.
H8521.origine: The Hebrew name תֵּל חַרְשָׁא is composed of תֵּל (tel), meaning 'mound' or 'archaeological hill', and חַרְשָׁא (harsha), which comes from the root denoting mutism or deafness. Thus, Thel-Harscha was a Babylonian site bearing a Semitic name that persisted long after its construction.
H8521.emploi: Thel-Harscha appears twice in the Bible, both in the lists of return from exile: in Ezra 2:59 and in Nehemiah 7:61 (the latter passage repeating the same list). It is among the cities of origin of the families returning from Babylon under Cyrus's reign, after the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar. The context is precise: these lists recorded who was returning to Judea and had to prove their legitimacy. The inhabitants of Thel-Harscha and neighboring localities could not demonstrate their authentic Israelite ancestry, placing them in a particular category among the repatriates.
H8521.portee: Thel-Harscha reminds us of Israel's dispersion in foreign lands and the concrete difficulties of returning from exile. It illustrates how, even after the return, the community of God's people had to verify its identity and heritage. This historical detail also shows that the exiled people had settled in various Babylonian cities, and that the reconstruction of Israel had to face genuine issues of lineage and recognition.

sens: A case worn on the shoulder or belt to hold arrows
A set formed by the quiver and the arrows it contains
H8522.detail:
1. The quiver is a case, typically made of leather or rigid fabric, designed to store and transport arrows. It is worn suspended from the shoulder or attached to the belt of the hunter or warrior. In Genesis 27:3, Isaac asks Esau to take his weapons — his quiver and his bow — to go hunting: the quiver is the essential accessory for the hunter, allowing him to keep his projectiles within reach.
2. By extension, the word also refers to both the empty case and the case filled with arrows, as the equipment is not separated from its contents: saying "take your quiver" means "take your quiver with its arrows." This is a typical usage of language, where the containing object represents the whole.
H8522.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "suspending" or "hanging." The quiver is indeed what hangs from the shoulder of the hunter or warrior. It is a simple and concrete word, formed to designate an everyday object: a pouch or case suspended where one stores arrows to always have them available.
H8522.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible: in Genesis 27:3, when Isaac, now old and blind, sends his son Esau to hunt. He asks him to take his quiver and his bow — the two inseparable elements of the ancient hunter's armament. The context shows that the quiver is a basic piece of equipment, an integral part of the warrior's or hunter's arsenal in the ancient Near East.
H8522.portee: This word reminds the reader of the concrete reality of ancient life and how one prepared for hunting or combat. The quiver, a humble yet essential object, also symbolizes the equipment that God entrusts to us to fulfill our mission: having the right weapons means being ready for the task.

sens: which comes in numerical order after the second
rank or position occupied in third order
H8523A.detail:
1. The word simply denotes the number three in an ordered series: the third place, the third part. It is the ordinal numeral adjective corresponding to the number three. In Daniel 5:7, King Belshazzar promises to the one who reads the mysterious inscription on the wall to give him "the third place in the government of the kingdom" — a very high position after the king himself and perhaps a prime minister.
2. Used as a noun, it can refer to the third person or the third thing itself, not just the order: "the third" among several.
H8523A.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same root as the Hebrew שְׁלִישִׁ (shelishi, "third"), which itself is formed from שָׁלוֹשׁ (shalosh, "three"). The family of the word expresses the idea of a series or order: after the first and the second comes the third. It is an ordinal numeral adjective, like in French "premier," "deuxième," "troisième."
H8523A.emploi: This word appears only once in the preserved Aramaic New Testament in Daniel 5:7. It is used to describe a coveted political rank: the king offers anyone who can decipher the mysterious writing to be clothed in purple, to wear a gold chain, and to receive the third place in the government — a royal promise of high honor and authority.
H8523A.portee: This word reminds us that earthly positions and honors are relative: even "the third place" can be envied and desired. For the believer, it invites us to remember that only God distributes true honors and that human dignities, even prestigious ones, remain temporary.

sens: The number that comes after two, the number three in an ordered sequence
That which occupies the position three in an order, a succession, or a classification
H8523B.detail:
1. It is simply the number three expressed as an ordered position: after the first and the second comes the third. In Daniel 2:39, the prophet Daniel explains King Nebuchadnezzar's dream by describing successive kingdoms: after the kingdom of Babylon (the first) and that of the Medes-Persians (the second), a third kingdom of bronze will come that will dominate the earth. The word thus designates a specific rank in a sequence.
2. By extension, it refers to whatever occupies the third place in a hierarchy or enumeration. The usage here emphasizes order and progression: each kingdom arrives in its time, the third logically following the first two.
H8523B.origine: This word comes from the Hebrew root related to the number three. It is the ordinal form (the rank, the order) of the number three, just as the French "troisième" is the ordinal of the number "trois." This formation allows for the transition from simple counting to the notion of place, position, or rank in a succession.
H8523B.emploi: This word appears only once in the provided biblical text, in Daniel 2:39. It occurs in the major interpretation that Daniel gives of King Nebuchadnezzar's great dream. The context is eschatological: Daniel reveals to Nebuchadnezzar the succession of four world kingdoms that will follow according to the divine plan. The third kingdom is presented as an empire of bronze destined to dominate the whole earth, after the first (Babylon, of gold) and the second (Medes-Persians, of silver).
H8523B.portee: This word reminds us that the history of earthly kingdoms follows a pre-established order by God. For the Christian reader, it teaches that the succession of world empires is not random, but is part of the divine plan revealed in advance. It is an invitation to recognize that God controls history and that every event has its place in His design.

sens: That which rises above the ordinary level, in altitude or position
That which is eminent, exalted, of great importance or dignity
H8524.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes what is physically elevated, rising toward the sky. In Ezekiel 17:22, the "high and lofty" mountain where the branch of the cedar will be planted is a place that dominates, distinguished by its altitude. This is the basic idea: something that exceeds, that overlooks.

2. In a figurative sense, "high" can also express what is exalted, glorious, of great value or dignity. It is the moral or spiritual excellence that rises above the common. The image remains that of elevation, but it transitions from the physical to the spiritual.
H8524.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that literally means "to be elevated, to rise up." It expresses the idea of ascent, of eminence. In biblical Hebrew, several words from the same family describe elevation in all its aspects: what rises, what is sublime, what surpasses.
H8524.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 17:22. It qualifies the mountain where God promises to plant the branch of the royal cedar. It is a context of restoration and honor: what was destroyed will be raised up, planted in a place of eminence. The usage remains concrete and spatial, but loaded with theological significance: God establishes His plan in a place of dignity and height.
H8524.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's promises are always fulfilled in dignity and glory. When God restores, He places His work in a high, visible place, not in obscurity. It is an encouragement: God does not forget, and what He restores will be exalted.

sens: Furrow dug in the ground by the plow
Trace, boundary line in a tilled field
Image of what sprouts or develops in the heart like in cultivated soil
H8525.detail:
1. A furrow is a deep line that the plow digs into the ground to prepare the soil to receive seeds. This is the fundamental work of plowing: we see this in Psalms 65:11, where God waters the furrows and smooths the clods so that the earth becomes fertile and produces sprouts.
2. By extension, the furrow refers to the fields themselves, divided and marked by these lines. In Hosea 10:4 and 12:12, the furrows of the fields symbolize the territory, the space where the consequences of human actions accumulate — like a harvest reaped where one has sown.
3. Spiritually, the furrow evokes what is "sown" and sprouts within us: Job 31:38 uses this image to speak of guilt, as if the earth itself cries out against the one who oppresses it, for every injustice leaves its marks and will bear fruit.
H8525.origine: The Hebrew word תֶּלֶם (tèlèm) comes from a root that means "to dig" or "to split." It simply designates the line that the plowman traces in the soil with his plow — a mundane image for an agricultural people, but rich in symbolic meaning: what is dug, one places what one wants to grow there.
H8525.emploi: The word appears 5 times in biblical Hebrew, exclusively in poetic or prophetic texts (Job, Psalms, Hosea). It is never used in a purely figurative sense, but always in connection with the concrete image of tilled earth. In Psalms 65, it is an act of divine blessing. In Hosea, it is the earth itself that testifies against the injustice committed — the furrows receive the moral imprint of human actions. In Job 31, it is a call to God regarding justice: if the earth accuses, it is because there is indeed fault.
H8525.portee: This word invites the believer to see their conscience as a tilled land: everything sown there — lies, injustice, or on the contrary faithfulness — will bear fruit. It reminds us that our actions do not disappear, but carve out traces that will sprout. The Bible never isolates the furrow from the plowman: the image reminds us that God sees what is done in secret, and that creation itself bears witness to our conduct.

sens: One of the three giant sons of Anak, living in Hebron at the time of the conquest of Canaan
H8526G.detail: Talmai was one of the three sons of the giant Anak who lived in Hebron when the Israelites arrived in Canaan (Numbers 13:22). He is mentioned alongside his brothers Sheshai and Ahiman. These three giants were killed by the men of Judah during the conquest of the land: Caleb drove them out of Hebron (Joshua 15:14), and the tribe of Judah defeated them in battle (Judges 1:10).
H8526G.origine: The name Talmai means "of the furrows" or "tilled," probably an image evoking the earth or physical strength. It is a Semitic name from the ancient times of Canaan, borne by giants who embodied the ancient power of the land before the Israelites conquered it.
H8526G.emploi: Talmai appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. He is first mentioned among the giants that the explorers sent by Moses saw in Hebron (Numbers 13:22). The Book of Joshua reports that Caleb drove these three giants from the territory that had been given to him (Joshua 15:14). The book of Judges finally describes how the tribe of Judah defeated them in direct combat (Judges 1:10). These three occurrences show how God granted victory to the Israelites over the giant inhabitants of the land.
H8526G.portee: Talmai represents the powerful and ancient enemy that God allows believers to conquer. His story encourages trust in the divine promise: despite his formidable strength, this giant yielded before the people of Israel, showing that victory comes from God and not from human strength.

sens: King of Geshur, father of Maacah and grandfather of Absalom
H8526H.detail: Talmai is a king of the small Aramean kingdom of Geshur, located east of the Jordan. He is best known as the father of Maacah, one of King David's wives, who became the mother of Prince Absalom (2 Samuel 3:3). When Absalom killed his half-brother Amnon, he fled from David's court and took refuge with his grandfather Talmai in Geshur, where he stayed for three years (2 Samuel 13:37). Talmai thus represents an external ally of the royal house of Israel, linked to David through marriage.
H8526H.origine: The name Talmai literally means "furrowed" or "tilled" in Hebrew, an image evoking a fertile field. It is a typical Aramean name of the northern kings, reflecting the political contacts between Israel and neighboring Aramean kingdoms in the first millennium B.C.
H8526H.emploi: Talmai appears three times in the Old Testament, always in relation to the royal family of David. He is first presented as king of Geshur and father of Maacah, one of the seven women who bore sons to David during his reign in Hebron (2 Samuel 3:3). His political importance increases during the Absalom affair: after the murder of Amnon, Prince Absalom flees to his grandfather Talmai to escape David's vengeance (2 Samuel 13:37). This flight reveals that Geshur was powerful enough and independent to offer refuge to the son of the king of Israel. The text of 1 Chronicles 3:2 confirms this genealogy by listing Absalom among the sons of David.
H8526H.portee: The story of Talmai reminds us that political and marital alliances played a crucial role in the ancient Near East. It also shows how the family crises of King David — such as Absalom's crime — had international repercussions and how divine providence even used foreign kingdoms to protect and guide the descendants of David.

sens: one who receives teaching from a master
one who learns a craft or trade from an expert
one who follows the doctrine or cause of someone
H8527.detail: 1. A disciple is primarily one who learns directly from a master. In 1 Chronicles 25:8, we see "masters and disciples" in the service of the Temple: these are experienced musicians teaching younger ones their craft, and the apprentices receiving this teaching. 2. The word more broadly designates one who is trained in a trade or skill by imitating an expert and practicing under their guidance. 3. In a figurative and deeper sense, a disciple is one who adheres to the thought, teaching, or cause of a master and commits to follow and live according to their principles.
H8527.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to learn" or "to study." It describes one who is engaged in a process of learning, transmitting knowledge from an expert to one who progresses. The same root is found in other Hebrew words related to study and instruction.
H8527.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament (1 Chronicles 25:8), in the specific context of musical service in the Temple. It designates the apprentice musicians learning from their masters. It is a word that gained significant importance in the New Testament, where it describes the apostles and followers of Jesus, but in the Old Testament it remains limited to this single passage on the transmission of musical know-how in worship.
H8527.portee: This word reminds us that learning and transmission are at the heart of community life, especially in worship. For the Christian, it invites reflection on the importance of the roles of master and learner: each grows by receiving from others and sharing what they have received.

sens: Babylonian locality from which exiles returned at the time of Zerubbabel
H8528.detail: 1. Thel-Mélach is a place located in Babylon from which some Israelite exiles returned during the time of Zerubbabel (around 538 B.C.). The name literally means "mound of salt." It is a geographically identifiable site in ancient Mesopotamia (Ezra 2:59).
H8528.origine: The Hebrew name תֵּל תֵּל (tel) means a mound or hill, often formed by the accumulated remains of ancient dwellings. The second element מֶלַח (melah) means "salt." Together, it designates a mound or region marked by salt deposits, evoking the arid landscapes of Babylon and the ancient Near East. This type of geographical name was common in Mesopotamia.
H8528.emploi: Thel-Mélach appears only twice in the Bible, both times in direct relation to the return from exile. It is listed in the two parallel lists of exiles who returned with Zerubbabel: that of Ezra 2 and that of Nehemiah 7. In both cases, Thel-Mélach is mentioned alongside other Babylonian localities (Thel-Harscha, Kerub-Addan/Addon) as a starting point for groups of exiles whose Israelite genealogy could not be established with certainty. These people had lost track of their "ancestral home" and their "lineage," which made them suspect regarding their legitimacy to return to Israel and participate in the restoration of the temple.
H8528.portee: Thel-Mélach reminds the reader that the return from exile did not gather only pure-blooded Israelites: people of diverse origins, who passed through Babylon, also made the journey back. This indicates the demographic complexity of the returning community and the necessity for religious authorities to verify genealogies. It is a humble reminder that the restoration of Jerusalem was also built with men and women whose past was uncertain.

sens: To be clothed in purple, in scarlet-dyed fabric
To wear the attire of a warrior or noble
H8529.detail:
1. The word literally means to be dressed or clothed in purple, this highly prized scarlet dye in antiquity. Purple was a luxurious and expensive color, reserved for high-ranking warriors, leaders, and kings. In Nahum 2:4, the prophet describes the Assyrian warriors appearing on the battlefield dressed in purple, emphasizing their warrior status and wealth.
2. Figuratively, it evokes the appearance and dignity of the fighter: one who wears purple is recognized as a man of power and prestige, clothed with the authority of battle.
H8529.origine: The Hebrew word תָּלַע (talâ) comes from a root that evokes the idea of dressing or covering. In Nahum, it is used in the Pual, a passive form that emphasizes the action of being dressed rather than dressing oneself. This purple dye came from the murex, a marine mollusk, and its production was labor-intensive: this is why it symbolized luxury and high social rank in the ancient Near East.
H8529.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Nahum 2:4. The prophet Nahum describes the march of the Assyrian troops against Nineveh, and the purple of the warriors is a detail that enhances the image of their power and arrogance before the city's fall. The context is one of imminent destruction, and this wealth of clothing appears as a fleeting vanity in the face of divine judgment.
H8529.portee: This word reminds the reader that even human prestige and the luxury of the powerful are but fragile appearances before God. Nahum uses this bright color to paint the grandeur of the Assyrian empire at the moment it is about to collapse, inviting the believer not to fear the great ones of this world.

sens: Place or structure where weapons and armor are stored
Collection of weapons and military equipment of a city or army
(Figuratively) Resources or means of defense
H8530.detail:
1. An arsenal is a building or fortification where weapons, shields, and military equipment are stored and preserved. The text of Song of Solomon 4:4 describes the neck of a young woman as a tower like that of David, equipped with an arsenal: it is the image of a structure where a thousand shields are hung, evoking a well-defended fortress.
2. The word also designates the complete set of weapons and armor available to a city or army for protection and combat. This collection of military equipment represents the power and defensive capability of a people.
3. Figuratively, the arsenal symbolizes the resources, means, or defenses one has in the face of adversity. In the poetic passage of the Song, the image compares the beauty and solidity of the woman's neck to a fortified tower equipped with all its means of protection.
H8530.origine: The Hebrew word תַּלְפִּיָּוֹת (talpiyyot) appears in a descriptive composition that evokes towers or defensive structures filled with weapons. Its precise etymology remains debated among scholars, but the image evoked is clearly that of an armament and defense site. The plural form of the word emphasizes the idea of multiplicity: several weapons, several shields, several means of protection gathered in one place.
H8530.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the love poem of the Song of Songs (4:4). The author uses it poetically to praise the beauty and strength of the beloved, comparing features of her body to impressive architectural and military elements. The context of the Song, which is a song of praise and admiration, transforms the usual military term into an image of protection, solidity, and beauty. This unique usage in Scripture makes the word particularly interesting for understanding the highly imagistic and poetic style of the Song.
H8530.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the poetic language of Scripture: the Bible uses strong images drawn from everyday and military life to express beauty and admiration. For the believer, the image of the arsenal also reminds that defense and protection are gifts from God, and that true strength lies in His support. This passage shows how human love, in its carnal and spiritual dimension, is celebrated in Scripture without reservation or shame.

sens: the number 3, one of three
the rank that comes after two others in an order
a fraction equal to one third of the whole
H8531.detail:
1. The word designates the number 3 or what occupies the third position in a series. In Daniel 5:16, King Nebuchadnezzar promises Daniel that he "will have the third place in the government of the kingdom" — that is, the third rank of power after two other dignitaries.
2. By extension, it indicates a rank or dignity: Daniel receives this third dignity as a reward for his skill in interpreting the mysterious writing on the wall. It is a position of honor, although inferior to the first two.
3. The word can also mean a part or portion equal to one third (although this meaning is not illustrated in the provided usages, it adds to the ordinal notion).
H8531.origine: This Aramaic word is the form of the Hebrew "shélishi" (the third), which comes from the root "shàlosh" (three). Aramaic was the administrative language of the Persian empire, and Belshazzar is an example: Daniel, serving at the court of the Babylonian then Persian king, hears and speaks the official Aramaic.
H8531.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, in verses 16 and 29 of chapter 5 of Daniel. Both occurrences echo each other: first, the king promises Daniel to give him this third place if he can read and explain the writing on the wall (verse 16), then he fulfills his promise (verse 29). It is an administrative term from the Babylonian royal context.
H8531.portee: This passage shows how Daniel's wisdom and faithfulness earn him recognition and honor in the eyes of the kings of the world, even if these honors remain far from his true vocation: to serve the God of Israel. The reader discovers that he who honors the true God can also be honored by the powerful — but true honor comes from God alone.

sens: the cardinal number 3
the ordinal position: third
H8532.detail:
1. The word simply designates the number three, in its sense of quantity: "three men" (Daniel 3:23), "three officials" (Daniel 6:2), or "three rows of stones" (Ezra 6:4). It is the number that comes after two.
2. It can also express order or position: "third day" (Ezra 6:15) means the day that comes after the second. In the Aramaic Bible, this same word carries both meanings without a clear distinction — it is the context that determines.
H8532.origine: The word comes from the ancient Semitic root tlt, which means "three" in several ancient Middle Eastern languages. In classical Hebrew, the form שָׁלוֹשׁ (shalom) is found; Aramaic uses תְּלָת (telat), which is the form from the eastern dialect. This root is very ancient and is related to the idea of "group of three," without any particular starting image — it is simply the number itself.
H8532.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Aramaic Bible, almost exclusively in the later books of Ezra and Daniel. It is used to count concrete objects (rows of stones, officials, men), but also to mark moments in time (days) and frequencies ("three times a day" in Daniel 6:10, where Daniel regularly prays three times). The nuance between the cardinal sense (how many) and ordinal sense (which rank) depends entirely on the context: "three men" is cardinal, "third day" is ordinal. In Daniel, the number three often appears when counting the horns of a beast (Daniel 7:5, 7:8, 7:20, 7:24), giving the number a certain significance in the apocalyptic vision.

sens: the number 30
H8533.detail: 1. The number thirty, used in the book of Daniel to designate a specific period of time. In Daniel 6:7 and 6:12, it refers to the royal decree prohibiting prayers to any god or man for thirty days, except to King Darius — a time frame set to test the loyalty of the subjects of the kingdom.
H8533.origine: This Aramaic word תְּלָתִין (telatin) is the Aramaic equivalent of the Hebrew word שְׁלֹשִׁים (sheloushim, "thirty"). It comes from the same Semitic root designating the number three, from which the formation of the number thirty (three times ten) is derived. The book of Daniel, partially written in Aramaic, uses the Aramaic forms of common numbers and figures.
H8533.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Daniel 6, in the context of the famous decree against Daniel. The expression "thirty days" recurs identically in verses 7 and 12, forming an inclusion that emphasizes the importance and irrevocability of this royal decree. It is a limited time frame, allowing the king to assert his supremacy over the kingdom.
H8533.portee: This number delineates the critical period during which Daniel must choose between obeying the king's decree or remaining faithful to his prayer addressed to God alone. For the reader, these thirty days symbolize the trial of faith and the steadfastness in religious conviction in the face of political pressure.

sens: The wavy and free hair of a woman
Hair that moves in the wind, light and supple
H8534.detail: 1. The word designates hair that is not straight or tight, but naturally waves and floats gracefully. In Song of Solomon 5:11, the poet describes the beloved: "Her curls are flowing, black as a raven" — it is the image of abundant, lively hair that moves freely and catches the light like waves.
H8534.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that suggests undulation and movement. The reduplicated form (tal-tal) reinforces this idea of waves or curls that repeat and snake. This structure of repetition is typical in Hebrew to express a quality that extends, prolongs, multiplies. The image is of hair that is not smooth, but curly or wavy, giving an impression of movement and life.
H8534.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 5:11. It is used to describe the hair of the beloved in the context of a poetic celebration of her beauty. It is a rare term, likely related to the world of lyrical poetry and personal description, rather than to ordinary or technical usage.
H8534.portee: This word invites us to appreciate beauty in its natural and vibrant form. In the Song, it emphasizes that beauty does not reside in rigidity or constraint, but in the grace of movement and freedom. For the believer, this can remind us that God loves authentic and overflowing life, that which floats freely, rather than what is forced or artificial.

sens: Complete, whole, without defect
Solid, well-built, well-assembled
Innocent, morally pure, without guilt
Upright, honest, of moral integrity
H8535.detail:
1. Complete, whole, without defect: the word describes something or someone that lacks nothing, possessing all its qualities. In Exodus 36:29, the boards of the tabernacle are "firmly joined" at their top — they form a complete and well-assembled whole.
2. Solid, well-built, well-assembled: it conveys the idea that the parts are joined firmly and durably. The structures of the tabernacle that Moses builds are thus "joined" together to form a stable whole.
3. Innocent, morally pure, without guilt: the person of integrity has nothing to reproach, they bear no guilt. Job himself declares in Job 9:21: "Innocent! I am," expressing his conviction that his conscience is clear before God.
4. Upright, honest, of moral integrity: it is the quality of one who acts with uprightness, who does not deviate from the moral path. Job 1:8 describes him as: "a man of integrity and uprightness, fearing God and turning away from evil" — someone whose entire life is marked by honesty and the fear of God.
H8535.origine: The Hebrew word tam comes from a root that means "to be complete, whole, finished." It expresses the idea of wholeness, absence of break or flaw. In the Hebrew Bible, this word can qualify both a material thing (a well-assembled structure) and a moral person (someone with a right heart). The integrity described here is not a flawless perfection, but rather the completeness of a person who walks in uprightness and hides nothing.
H8535.emploi: This word appears 16 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the wisdom books (Job and Psalms) and in Genesis and Exodus. It primarily qualifies a moral quality: Job is the major example (Job 1:1, 1:8, 2:3), presented as "integrity and uprightness." The psalmist uses it to exhort to observe "the one who is upright" (Psalms 37:37). Genesis 25:27 applies it to Jacob, described as "quiet" — calm, sedentary, different from the fiery Esau. In Exodus 36:29, the word applies to things: the boards of the tabernacle are "joined" together. The meaning thus oscillates between moral integrity and material solidity, but the common idea is that of completeness and absence of flaw.
H8535.portee: The word invites the believer to seek integrity: a coherent life where actions and words align with the fear of God. Job is the model — not someone perfect or without suffering, but someone whose conscience is right and heart sincere. It is an exhortation not to be divided internally, not to have a double life, but to walk in clarity and honesty before God and before men.

sens: Physical location or area where something is found or occurs
Residence or dwelling of a person or deity
H8536.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a specific location or area: it is where one seeks something, stands, or acts. In Ezra 6:6, the governor orders his colleagues to stay away from the "place" of the temple under reconstruction, meaning the precise location where the work is taking place.
2. The word takes on a more noble dimension when referring to the dwelling of a deity: in Ezra 6:12, "this place" refers to the temple in Jerusalem as the location where the God of Israel "causes His name to dwell" — that is, the place where He chooses to manifest His presence and power.
H8536.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the Hebrew verb "to be there"; it is a direct cousin of the Hebrew word for "there" (שָׁם, sham) found in many texts of the Old Testament. Aramaic and Hebrew share this root that simply expresses the idea of presence in a location. In the Greek translations of the Old Testament, this word often has an equivalent that carries the same meaning: a simple adverb or noun to designate a space.
H8536.emploi: This Aramaic word appears four times in the book of Ezra, which recounts the return of the exiles after the Babylonian captivity (around 520 B.C.). It is found in the royal edicts of King Darius and in official correspondence regarding the reconstruction of the temple. In Ezra 6:1, they search the archives; in 6:6 and 6:12, they speak of the place of the temple. In these political and religious contexts, the word retains its concrete meaning of location, but it always carries the spiritual significance of God's presence in the temple.
H8536.portee: This simple word reminds us that biblical faith is never purely abstract: it is lived in a place, it is embodied. The temple is a real location where God chooses to manifest His presence. For Christians, this resonates differently — the temple is now the body of the believer or the assembly — but the principle remains: our relationship with God is not floating; it has weight, reality, an "address."

sens: Completeness, wholeness, absence of lack
Moral purity, innocence of heart
Uprightness in conduct, honesty
Simplicity, candor, absence of deceit
H8537.detail: 1. Integrity primarily refers to the completeness or wholeness of something — nothing lacking, nothing damaged. It is the image of an intact totality: a pure and complete heart, without cracks or divisions. Abimelech says in Genesis 20:5 that he acted "with a pure heart," meaning without hidden malice, in moral completeness. 2. Integrity signifies innocence: an absence of guilt, intentional wrongdoing. One who walks in integrity has not committed evil. Psalms 25:21 and 41:13 associate innocence and uprightness with God's protection. 3. It is the uprightness of life, honesty in daily conduct: the person of integrity acts according to what is right, not swayed by profit or appearance. Proverbs 10:9 and 13:6 show that walking in integrity protects, while perverting the path leads to ruin. 4. Integrity also suggests sincerity without calculation, the candor of one who does not play both sides. David walks "with a sincere heart" before God (1 Kings 9:4), meaning without ulterior motives.
H8537.origine: The Hebrew word תֹּם comes from a root expressing the idea of finitude, completeness. It describes a finished state, a whole that needs no addition. In the Hebrew Bible, integrity is a central virtue: it designates the moral state of one who is whole, consistent, without double nature. It is a quality of those who seek to please God by living according to His laws without deviation or deceit.
H8537.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, Proverbs, and some historical narratives. It characterizes primarily the righteous: Job, Abimelech, David in times of uprightness. Proverbs regularly celebrates it: one who walks in integrity finds wisdom and protection (Proverbs 2:7, 10:9, 19:1). The Psalms invoke it as a shield against traps (Psalms 25:21, 26:1). Integrity contrasts with duplicity, the perversion of the path: it is not naive innocence, but a deliberate uprightness, a choice to live whole and loyal to God and others.
H8537.portee: Biblical integrity calls the believer to inner unity: no double game between professed faith and hidden life. It is to walk before God without deviation, in coherent actions and words. This virtue promises protection and honor — God supports those who seek to live uprightly. For today's disciple, it is a call to authentic sincerity, far from masks and compromises.

sens: State of a whole person, without flaw, in moral conduct and principles
Faithfulness to righteousness and good, even under temptation or suffering
Innocence, absence of guilt before God
H8538.detail:
1. Integrity refers to the quality of a person whose heart and actions are united, coherent, without duplicity. It is to be whole, not divided between professed principles and hidden conduct. Job tells his friends: "Until my last breath, I will defend my innocence" (Job 27:5), meaning he refuses to renounce the integrity that has always characterized him.
2. Integrity is also this moral firmness that perseveres even under pain and trial. When Job's wife urges him to give up, he "remains steadfast in his integrity" (Job 2:9): he refuses to curse God out of despair, as that would betray his true relationship with Him. It is integrity as constancy of heart.
