In Numbers 14:34, it describes the consequence of Israel's lack of trust: the deprivation of divine presence for forty years in the desert is the price of their opposition. In Job 33:10, it expresses the divine hostility perceived by the suffering righteous: God seems to become an adversary. In both cases, the context is one of punishment or suffering, and opposition primarily signifies a rupture in the normal relationship between God and His people.
H8569.portee: This word reminds the believer that opposition to God bears bitter fruit: the deprivation of His presence is the gravest punishment. It shows that what one refuses to the Lord — obedience, trust, submission — is ultimately refused to oneself, for communion with God is the source of all blessing. For one who suffers unjustly, it also speaks of the mystery of divine silence: sometimes, God seems to oppose us, but this appearance hides a wisdom and justice that we do not see at first glance.

sens: What a tree or plant produces: grain, harvest, crop
Food that the earth provides for man
Image of prosperity and divine blessing
H8570.detail: 1. The fruit is primarily the natural product of a tree or plant: it is what grows and ripens, ready to be eaten. When the fig tree speaks of its "excellent fruit" (Judges 9:11), it refers to the sweetness of the fig itself, that tasty food it bears. 2. By extension, this word designates everything the earth produces to nourish man: the grain from the fields, the harvest. Those who perish from hunger are "deprived of the fruit of the fields" (Lamentations 4:9), meaning cut off from the harvest that would feed them. 3. Finally, the fruit becomes an image of blessing: when God blesses, the earth "fills the world with its fruits" (Isaiah 27:6), a symbol of prosperity and life. It is the visible sign that the Lord grants His help to His people.
H8570.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes production, growth. It belongs to the family of words that speak of what "grows" and "germinates." In itself, it is very concrete: it simply designates what a plant gives, before taking on a broader and figurative meaning.
H8570.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Old Testament, mostly in poetic and prophetic texts. Deuteronomy 32:13 uses it for the harvests that Israel reaps on the heights: it is the promised material blessing. Isaiah 27:6 uses it figuratively: the people of God, rooted and alive, "fills the world with its fruits," a symbol of spiritual and material fertility. Ezekiel 36:30 promises that God "will multiply the fruit of the trees and the produce of the fields," announcing renewal after punishment. Each time, the word carries a charge of blessing or, conversely, its absence signifies misfortune.
H8570.portee: This word reminds the believer that life, food, and prosperity come from God alone. When the Bible speaks of "fruit," it invites us to see in every harvest, in every crop, the benevolent work of the Lord. It is also an invitation to recognize that our own spiritual fertility — our deeds, our testimonies — exists only if we remain rooted in God, just as a plant is rooted in the soil.

sens: the fleshy and rounded part that hangs at the bottom of the ear
in anointing rituals, the part of the body touched to consecrate or purify
H8571.detail:
1. The lobe is the soft and fleshy part that hangs from the bottom of the ear: it is this visible part, often adorned with earrings in women (Leviticus 8:23).
2. In the sacred rituals of the Bible, the lobe of the right ear becomes a symbolic point of contact: God commands that blood or consecrated oil be placed there during the consecration of priests or the purification of the sick. It is an act that places the whole person — from the upper body to the lower (ear, hand, foot) — under divine anointing (Exodus 29:20; Leviticus 14:14-17).
H8571.origine: The Hebrew word תְּנוּךְ comes from a root that designates something that hangs or is suspended, the idea of a soft and hanging part. The lobe, literally, is this soft and malleable portion of the ear that contrasts with the more rigid structure of the rest of the ear.
H8571.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Bible, only in the books of Leviticus and Exodus, all in ritual contexts of purification or consecration. It is always accompanied by 'right' and associated with two other parts of the body (the thumb of the right hand and the big toe of the right foot). These passages describe the anointing of the priest Aaron and his sons during their consecration (Exodus 29:20; Leviticus 8), and the anointing of healed lepers who are being purified (Leviticus 14). The repetition of the trio (ear, hand, foot) suggests a total mark: the anointing touches the symbol of listening (ear), action (hand), and walking (foot).
H8571.portee: For the Christian, these passages show that biblical consecration is not an abstract formula: it is embodied, concrete, it touches the whole body. The anointing of the lobe of the ear means that we are called to listen to the word of God with our whole being. The repetition of this gesture on the right side emphasizes that our consecration is done under the gaze and blessing of God.

sens: State of light sleep, half-sleep
Numbness that overtakes one who closes their eyes
Laziness, inaction of one who gives in to rest
Fleeting moment of rest
H8572.detail:
1. Assoupissement is primarily a shallow sleep, an intermediate state between wakefulness and deep sleep. This is what God uses to speak to man: 'He speaks in dreams, in visions of the night, when deep sleep falls upon men, when they slumber on their beds' (Job 33:15). It is a sleep in which one remains half-conscious, accessible to visions.
2. The word also designates the numbness of the eyelids, that feeling of heaviness that rises when one is sleepy and struggles to stay awake. One who wants to remain vigilant refuses this assoupissement: 'I will not give sleep to my eyes, nor slumber to my eyelids' (Psalms 132:4).
3. By extension, assoupissement becomes an image of laziness and inaction. One who gives in to rest at the wrong moment accumulates small moments of abandonment: 'A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest!' (Proverbs 6:10). It is the laziness that sleeps within us and weakens us.
4. Finally, the word evokes those fleeting moments of rest, those brief moments when one closes their eyes — crumbs of sleep that, repeated, become ruinous for one who must keep watch over their affairs.
H8572.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means 'to doze off' or 'to nap'. It belongs to the family of words designating sleep and rest, but with a specific nuance: it is a partial sleep, a transition between wakefulness and deep sleep. This nuance makes it a particularly expressive word for speaking of the vulnerability of one who only sleeps halfway, or of the weakness of one who yields to the small calls of rest.
H8572.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the Wisdom literature (Proverbs and Job). In Job 33:15, it designates the state conducive to divine revelation, the moment when God can instruct man through visions. In Proverbs, it takes on a critical connotation: assoupissement becomes the symbol of laziness (Proverbs 6:4 and 6:10, repeated in 24:33), those small moments of rest that, accumulated, ruin the slothful. Psalm 132:4 makes it a symbol of religious vigilance, of zeal not to relax. The context thus varies from the favorable reception of sleep (when God speaks) to its vigorous rejection (when one must remain vigilant).
H8572.portee: This word speaks to every believer who knows the temptation of laziness, even spiritual laziness. Assoupissement represents those moments when one relaxes, when one lets their guard down — moments that, if repeated, can weaken our entire life. But the word also reminds us that sleep is not bad in itself: it is when God speaks to the drowsy man that He can instruct him. It is therefore a matter of discerning the moment: vigilance when action is needed, openness when God speaks to us.

sens: Action of waving or shaking something back and forth
Gift presented to God while holding it at arm's length and moving it before the Lord
Portion of the sacrifices reserved for the priests in Israelite worship
Gesture of consecration and solemn presentation to God
Figuratively: movement, trembling, agitation
H8573.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the physical gesture: to shake, to wave, to move back and forth. It is a repeated movement back and forth, like when one shakes an object (Exodus 29:24: 'you shall wave them back and forth before the Lord').
2. As a waved offering, it designates the specific ritual of Israelite worship: the priest holds in his hands a portion of the sacrificed animal or offerings and waves them before the Lord to consecrate them (Leviticus 8:27: Aaron waves the portions on the hands of his sons before God).
3. This action serves to solemnly present to the Lord the portion that belongs to the priests: it is a gesture of recognition and dedication (Leviticus 10:15: the breast 'that is waved back and forth before the Lord' becomes the portion for the priests).
4. The word also applies to other waved gifts, such as the sheaf on the day of Passover or the gold brought for the sanctuary (Leviticus 23:15: the sheaf 'waved back and forth'; Exodus 38:24: the gold of the 'offerings').
5. Figuratively, the word evokes agitation or trembling: Isaiah 30:32 speaks of blows struck 'in rhythm' (regular movement), and Isaiah 19:16 of the trembling of the Egyptians before the divine threat.
H8573.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that means 'to shake, to wave, to brandish'. This root evokes the physical gesture of moving an object back and forth in the air, hence the name of this type of offering characterized by this specific movement. The family of the word extends to terms also designating trembling and agitation. It is a technically sacrificial term: only the worship of Israel employs this ritual gesture, which symbolizes presentation and consecration before God.
H8573.emploi: The word appears 28 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the Torah (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers), where it describes the ritual of waved offerings. It is mostly used in the singular to designate the action or the offered portion: the priest waves the breast or shoulder of the sacrificed animal (Leviticus 7:30, 10:15), the sheaf during the harvest (Leviticus 23:15, 23:20), the gifts of the Levites (Numbers 8:11). In these contexts, it is the gesture that consecrates and purifies the portion intended for the priests or for the service of the tabernacle. In Isaiah, the word takes on a broader figurative sense: it evokes trembling or movement (19:16, 30:32), far from the cultic context.
H8573.portee: This word shows the importance of gesture in communion with God: it is not a gift thrown at the foot of the altar, but a living act, a presentation in movement that manifests reverence and personal offering. For today's Christian, it is a reminder that our relationship with God is not passive or distant, but active and engaged. Movement and intention accompany the gift.

sens: Construction or installation used for cooking or heating at very high temperatures
By extension, fortified tower or city gate bearing this name
H8574G.detail:
1. An oven is a closed structure heated intensely, used for baking bread or melting metals. It is an essential piece of equipment in any household or community. In Jerusalem, during the reconstruction of the walls under Nehemiah, there was a "tower of ovens" (Nehemiah 3:11), probably a defensive point near where public or artisanal ovens were located.
2. The name "Tower of Ovens" (Migdal Tannur) refers to a specific gate or bastion in Jerusalem. This fortified structure, mentioned during the dedication procession of the walls (Nehemiah 12:38), marked a well-known landmark in the city's topography.
H8574G.origine: The Hebrew word tannur literally means "oven" and likely comes from a root describing the action of heating or cooking. It is a simple word, with no apparent morphological links to other Hebrew words in the New Testament. The Greek fornax often translates this term in texts from the Second Temple period.
H8574G.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the book of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 3:11 and 12:38), where it specifically refers to the "Tower of Ovens," a part of the wall of Jerusalem rebuilt in the 5th century B.C. The expression "tower of ovens" or "gate of ovens" was likely the name of a well-known fortification to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, perhaps because it overlooked an area where public ovens were located or served both as a defensive point and access to cooking facilities.

sens: Cooking or heating device, generally made of stone or metal
Fiery furnace, blaze where an intense fire burns
Image of God's anger that consumes and destroys
Intense and burning desire, fervent passion
H8574H.detail:
1. The oven is primarily a practical device for baking bread and food: in Leviticus 2:4, offerings must be baked in the oven, showing that it is a common installation in homes or sanctuaries.

2. The word then evokes the intensity of heat and fire: when God establishes His covenant with Abraham in Genesis 15:17, a smoking furnace and flames pass between the animals, an impressive and terrifying image that manifests divine presence.

3. The Bible uses the oven as an image of divine anger that burns and destroys: in Psalms 21:10, God makes His enemies a fiery furnace, annihilating them in His anger; in Malachi 4:1, the day of judgment will be like a burning oven where the wicked will burn.

4. The word also describes intense human passions: in Hosea 7:6-7, the hearts of the conspirators are like an oven, an image of the burning desire that drives them to conspire; in Lamentations 5:10, hunger burns the skins like an oven, expressing extreme suffering.
H8574H.origine: The Hebrew word תַּנּוּר comes from a root that evokes ardor and heat. It originally designates a potter's oven or a baker's oven, a common utensil in the ancient Near East. The image of the oven — a closed space where an intense fire burns — has naturally lent itself to figurative uses to describe anger, passion, or suffering. The Greeks translated this word as fornax in Latin and as kaminos in Greek, terms that retain this same range of meanings.
H8574H.emploi: The word appears thirteen times in the Old Testament, primarily to describe cooking ovens (Leviticus 2:4; 7:9; 11:35), but it is most often used figuratively in the Psalms and the prophets. In Genesis 15:17, it symbolizes the manifestation of God; in Psalms 21:10 and Malachi 4:1, it represents divine judgment; in Hosea 7:4-7, it describes the fervor of human passions and plots; in Lamentations 5:10, it expresses the burning of hunger and suffering. The context determines whether one is speaking of a concrete object or a spiritual reality: the common idea is always that of intense heat, destructive or purifying.
H8574H.portee: This word teaches the reader that God's anger, far from being cold or abstract, is a burning and inevitable reality for those who oppose Him. It also invites us to examine our own passions and desires: are they controlled, or do they burn like an uncontrolled oven? For the believer, the oven reminds us both that God judges with intensity and that He alone can preserve us from the coming judgment.

sens: Word, gesture, or presence that comforts someone in pain
Relief, alleviation of suffering
Comfort that God brings to the believer who suffers
H8575.detail:
1. The word first designates a concrete word or action that soothes an afflicted person. In Job 21:2, Job asks his friends to give him only this consolation of listening to his words — he seeks relief from his suffering through their attention. In Jeremiah 16:7, the cup of consolation is a ritual gesture of sharing offered to someone mourning a death.
2. More broadly, it is the comfort, the soothing that a person or presence brings. When in Psalms 94:19 troubled thoughts stir the heart, it is the consolations of God — His benevolent interventions — that rejoice the soul and calm it.
3. In a religious perspective, this word evokes divine comfort. In Isaiah 66:11, the people are invited to be nourished with the milk of the consolations of God, a poetic image where divine comfort is a food. In Job 15:11, the consolations of God are part of His words that gently reach the heart of the righteous.
H8575.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that means "to repent" or "to turn towards" — the underlying idea being a turning of the heart, a change of orientation. Consolation is what turns the heart away from suffering and towards hope. Other words in the same family carry the idea of compassion and a change of feeling.
H8575.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the books of wisdom and the prophets. It designates sometimes human consolation — that which we give to one another in the face of mourning (Jeremiah 16:7) — and more often, the divine consolation that only God can offer to those who suffer (Job 15:11; Psalms 94:19; Isaiah 66:11). The context is always one of suffering — grief, illness, mourning, injustice — and consolation is the remedy that soothes and restores trust.
H8575.portee: This word reminds believers that suffering is not the end: God offers His consolations to those who cry out to Him. It educates the heart to receive not complete explanations of suffering, but a comfort that supports and pacifies the soul. It is also a call to comfort one another in times of mourning, reflecting God's compassion.

sens: Father of Serajah, a military leader who rallied to Gedaliah after the fall of Jerusalem
H8576.detail: Tanhumeth is a man whose name means "consolation" in Hebrew. He is mentioned as the father of Serajah, one of the leaders of the troops who, after the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians in 586 B.C., went to Gedaliah whom the king of Babylon had appointed governor. Serajah and his men joined Gedaliah at Mizpah (2 Kings 25:23), an act of rallying to the authority established by Babylon. This same Serajah, son of Tanhumeth, is mentioned again in Jeremiah 40:8 among the officers and their troops who came to find Gedaliah after the fall of the city.
H8576.origine: The name Tanhumeth comes from the Hebrew root "nahom" which means "to console, to comfort." It is a theophoric name borne by one whose Lord was the consolation or who brought comfort to his people during a time of great national distress.
H8576.emploi: Tanhumeth is known only from these two biblical references, 2 Kings 25:23 and Jeremiah 40:8, which report practically the same event: the surrender of military leaders to Gedaliah after the capture of Jerusalem. He is identified exclusively as the father of Serajah and does not play an active role in the narrative himself. These two parallel passages show that his descendants, notably Serajah, integrated into the administration of the territory under Babylonian control.

sens: Carnivorous desert animal, related to the wolf
Wild creature that haunts ruins and desolate places
Image of desolation and divine judgment
H8577A.detail:
1. The jackal is a real animal found in the arid regions of the Middle East: it is a carnivore resembling a small wolf, which hunts at night and emits piercing cries. Job exclaims, "I have become a brother to jackals" (Job 30:29), expressing his extreme loneliness and misery by comparing himself to this rejected animal.
2. In the ruins of destroyed cities, jackals naturally settle: they inhabit deserted places and make them their lair. Scripture announces that Jerusalem will become "a haunt of jackals" (Jeremiah 9:11), as will Babylon (Jeremiah 51:37). This is a striking image of the total desolation of a once-prosperous city.
3. The jackal thus becomes a symbol of divine judgment: its presence marks the complete absence of human life, absolute ruin. When Isaiah prophesies that "jackals will howl in the palaces" (Isaiah 13:22), he paints the end of a proud civilization, replaced by the wild cries of beasts.
H8577A.origine: The Hebrew word תַּן (tan) designates this animal recognizable by its characteristic nocturnal calls. The Bible mentions it mainly in prophecies of ruin and desolation. A variant of the same word, תַּנָּה (tannah), means "dragon" or monstrous creature, perhaps evoking a larger or more terrifying animal. The image of the jackal in ruins was familiar to biblical readers of the ancient Near East.
H8577A.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Bible, primarily in the prophets (Jeremiah, Isaiah, Micah). It describes both a real desert animal and a figure of destruction. In Jeremiah 14:6, the jackals "pant for air like jackals" during drought, showing that even these beasts suffer when water disappears. The word is mainly used to announce that cities would become "heaps of ruins" (Jeremiah 9:11, 51:37): the jackal taking possession of the debris symbolizes the fulfillment of judgment. In Job 30:29, it is a creature of solitude and distress. Everywhere, it is an animal of abandoned places, never a companion or ally.
H8577A.portee: The jackal reminds us that divine judgment is real and fearsome: a magnificent city can become a desert haunted by wild beasts. This image warns us of the vanity of human pride and the importance of listening to the voice of God. It also invites us to recognize that spiritual loneliness and misery are a terrifying state: when Job compares himself to the jackal, he helps us understand the abyss of suffering and the need for compassion.

sens: Fabulous creature endowed with superhuman powers, terrifying and malevolent
Source of water or place bearing a threatening name
Image of monstrous and chaotic power
H8577B.detail: 1. The dragon is a legendary, terrifying creature associated with chaos and evil in biblical imagination. The Hebrew word *tannim* can also refer to monstrous serpents or fearsome sea creatures — beings that embody hostile power and threat. 2. In the context of Nehemiah 2:13, "the dragon's spring" is likely a place in Jerusalem known by this ominous name, located near the dung gate: this name may reflect either the presence of a wild and gushing spring or simply a sinister reputation attached to this location. 3. Even in a figurative sense, the dragon symbolizes what exceeds ordinary nature, what is great, fearsome, and belongs to the realm of the supernatural — an image of the power of evil that only God can overcome.
H8577B.origine: The word *tannim* (plural: *taninim*) comes from a root that evokes stretching, unfolding — the idea of a long and sinuous creature. It is an ancient Near Eastern term, adopted by biblical Hebrew to name fabulous beasts or large sea creatures. The word also appears to designate crocodiles or giant snakes, showing how biblical imagination placed dragons at the boundary between natural reality and the world of the marvelous.
H8577B.emploi: The word appears only once in the form *tannim* in Nehemiah 2:13, where it designates a geographical location in Jerusalem: "the dragon's spring." It is a place name that suggests either a dangerous or tumultuous water source or a location known for its evil associations. The context of Nehemiah's visit, inspecting the ruined walls of the holy city, gives this name a tone of desolation and threat — the dragon lurks near the ruins.
H8577B.portee: For the Christian reader, the dragon represents the power of evil and chaos, always present in the world, but never beyond the control and authority of God. The mention of this place in Jerusalem invites us to see that even the holy city must confront hostile powers, and that it can only be restored through trust in the One who reigns over all that is monstrous and dark.

sens: Creeping reptile capable of biting and injecting venom
Legendary monster or fantastical animal of enormous size
Image of evil, cunning, and spiritual threat
H8577M.detail:
1. The most common meaning refers to a real venomous reptile that crawls on the ground: it is the creature encountered in nature. In Exodus 7:9-10, Aaron's staff turns into a serpent before Pharaoh — a miracle confirmed by the Egyptian magicians, who do the same. Deuteronomy 32:33 evokes the deadly venom of serpents, an image of malice.
2. The word also designates monstrous, gigantic, and terrifying creatures: the dragon or the sea monster from ancient tales. These creatures embody a frightful power, beyond ordinary creatures.
3. In biblical figurative usage, the serpent symbolizes the spiritual enemy, malicious cunning, and the threat of evil. Psalms 91:13 shows the believer treading upon the dragon — total victory over the power of the wicked.
H8577M.origine: The Hebrew word תַּנִּין (tannin) is related to terms designating fearsome aquatic creatures. Its basic image is that of a creeping, scaly, and dangerous creature. In biblical texts, the term can evoke both the ordinary reptile and the monsters of Mesopotamian and Egyptian myths, of which the Hebrews were aware. The Old Testament sometimes adopts these cosmic images to speak of creation and the defeat of evil.
H8577M.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Segond. Three occurrences focus on Exodus 7:9-12, where the staff becomes a serpent — a foundational miracle at the threshold of Egypt. Deuteronomy 32:33 uses it in the sense of venom, deadly poison that kills. Psalms 91:13 makes it the adversary of the protected believer, one whom he treads upon. The word thus plays on two registers: the realism of the dangerous beast (Exodus, Deuteronomy) and the spiritual dimension of the battle against evil (Psalms). The staff turned into a serpent announces the multiplication of plagues and divine dominion over Egyptian power.
H8577M.portee: This word reminds the reader that God has authority over all that is living and threatening — even the most terrifying creatures obey His word. The transformation of the staff into a serpent shows the supernatural nature of divine power. For the believer, Psalms 91:13 offers the assurance that divine protection places him above what ordinarily threatens: he walks on danger without being harmed.

sens: Gigantic and fearsome aquatic creature, serpent or beast of the waters
Primitive or legendary animal of the abyss
Creature symbolizing the hostile power of nature or evil
H8577N.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to the large marine creatures that God created on day 5: these are real living animals, impressive in their size and strength (Genesis 1:21 calls them "fish"). 2. It also applies to the leviathan or crocodile, these serpents or beasts of superhuman power that inhabit the waters or rivers (Isaiah 27:1, Ezekiel 29:3). 3. In hymns and praise poems, these creatures become a symbol of the chaotic force that only God can control: they embody the hostility of the world against divine power (Psalms 74:13, Psalms 148:7). 4. Metaphorically, the monster represents the powerful enemy or threat that oppresses — Job mentions it to express his weakness against an adversary: why does God impose such surveillance on him (Job 7:12).
H8577N.origine: The Hebrew word tanin comes from a root expressing the idea of stretching, twisting: the image is that of a serpent writhing or a creature elongating in the water. It also appears in other Semitic languages with the meaning of serpent or wild beast. The leviathan, mentioned alongside the tanin in the Bible, is probably a specific tanin or a personified river.
H8577N.emploi: The word tanin appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in poems and passages that speak of creation or God's power. In Genesis 1:21, it is an animal created like the others, impressive but not evil. In the Psalms and Isaiah, the tanin becomes a symbol: it represents the powers of disorder or oppression that God conquers or controls. In Ezekiel 29:3 and Jeremiah 51:34, the tanin represents Egypt or Babylon, enemy kingdoms. The meaning thus varies from the concrete (marine animal) to the figurative (enemy, hostile power).
H8577N.portee: This word invites the believer to contemplate God's wonderful and terrible creation: these sea monsters manifest His creative power. It also reminds that every force hostile to God, even overwhelming or terrifying, remains under His absolute control. For the oppressed believer, this image affirms that God does not abandon His enemies to victory.

sens: Which comes in second position in a list or succession
Which occupies the number two rank
H8578.detail:
1. This word designates what comes after the first in an order or sequence. In Daniel 7:5, it qualifies the second animal in the prophetic vision: after seeing a first animal (a lion), Daniel sees a "second" animal "like a bear." The ordinal number simply marks its place in the series of four beasts that appear successively.
2. The meaning is purely numerical: it is the way of counting, enumerating, or classifying several elements by giving each its rank.
H8578.origine: This word is Aramaic and comes from the Hebrew root שְׁנַ֫יִם (shnayim, "two"). Aramaic borrowed from Hebrew this notion of duality and derived the ordinal adjective "second." It is a simple word that reflects universal counting: after one comes two, and thus the second.
H8578.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 7:5, in the context of a very important prophetic vision. Daniel receives a vision of the four great beasts that symbolize future empires. The term "second" marks the transition from one beast to the next, the bear being the second creature in this succession. It is a simple enumerative marker in a passage where the repetition of elements serves to construct a prophecy.
H8578.portee: This word invites the reader to respect the order and succession that God proposes: in Daniel's prophetic vision, each animal "second," "third"… counts in the unfolding of future events. It reminds that history does not unfold randomly, but according to an ordered divine plan.

sens: A second occurrence of an action or event
Again, anew
H8579.detail:
1. The word literally designates the moment when something happens for the second time. In Daniel 2:7, the magicians respond "for the second time" to the king: they had already responded the first time (in verse 4), and here they respond again, a second time.
2. By extension, it means "again" or "anew" — the idea of repetition, of recommencement. The emphasis is on the repeated nature of the action rather than on a simple second ordered occurrence.
H8579.origine: This Aramaic word is formed from the root שְׁנַ֫יִם ("two" in Hebrew). Just as in French "deuxième" comes from "deux," the Aramaic word tinyanut expresses ordinality: what comes after the first. It is a way of saying "times two" or "in second place." The Aramaic of Daniel thus borrows the numerical structures of Hebrew.
H8579.emploi: This word appears only once in the entire Bible, in Daniel 2:7. It is a passage where the Chaldean magicians of King Nebuchadnezzar, challenged to reveal the king's dream, respond again to clarify their position: they ask the king to report the dream to them so they can give its interpretation. This context of repetition (a second response) explains the choice of the Aramaic word tinyanut.
H8579.portee: This word illustrates the persistence of the wise in the face of the impossible. The magicians do not give up; they respond a second time, seeking to solve the riddle. For the Christian reader, this reminds that insistence and repeated prayer are biblical — an example among others of the spiritual value of "returning" to God and perseverance in the face of challenges.

sens: Impure animal of the law of Moses, probably a water bird
Impure animal, probably a reptile or amphibian
Creature excluded from ritual consumption in the Old Testament
H8580.detail:
1. The Hebrew word designates an impure aquatic animal listed among the forbidden birds: it could refer to the swan, but also to the ibis, the coot, or a species of owl (Leviticus 11:18). The translation "swan" in the Segond reflects an ancient uncertainty about the precise identification of this bird.

2. The same word appears in a list of impure reptiles or amphibians (Leviticus 11:30), where it is translated as "chameleon": this suggests that Hebrew, like many ancient languages, grouped under one term creatures with varied impure characteristics, without always designating the same species.

3. In biblical practice, this word is only used to identify animals to be ritually avoided: it signals cultic impurity rather than precisely describing a known creature. Its exact meaning has been lost over time, and translators have had to choose among the impure animals of the ancient Near East.
H8580.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that perhaps evokes breath or unusual character. The Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, does not provide a unique equivalent: this shows that even in antiquity, the exact meaning was forgotten. The word belongs to the vocabulary of ritual purity, a key area of the Mosaic Law.
H8580.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, all in lists of the Law concerning impure animals (Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14). These lists enumerate the creatures that Israel must not eat, in order to remain pure before God. The usage varies from one translation to another: "swan" in Leviticus 11:18 and Deuteronomy 14:16, "chameleon" in Leviticus 11:30. This instability reflects the historical uncertainty about the exact animal designated by the Hebrew word in each context.
H8580.portee: For today's believer, this word reminds that the Law of Moses classified the living world according to a logic of purity and impurity that structured Israel's relationship with God. Although these ceremonial laws no longer apply to Christians according to the New Testament, they reveal God's holiness and the importance He attached to order and separation between the pure and the impure.

sens: To reject with disgust, to refuse with repugnance
To consider as impure or forbidden according to the Law
To act in a repugnant or dishonorable way
To inspire disgust in someone
H8581.detail:
1. To reject something or someone with an intense feeling of disgust and rejection. It is to hold a person or thing in horror, to find it odious. In Deuteronomy 7:26, Israel is to "abhor" the idols of the defeated peoples, to absolutely reject them as one would discard what is repugnant.
2. In religious language, it marks something as abominable according to the Law, to prohibit or condemn it as contrary to the will of God. A practice can be "abominable" in the eyes of the Lord: in 1 Chronicles 21:6, the census of the people appears as an "abomination" to King David.
3. To commit a shameful or repugnant act oneself, to act in a degrading manner. In Psalms 14:1, the foolish "commit abominable actions" by denying God and corrupting themselves.
4. To be the object of someone else's disgust, to inspire aversion. In Isaiah 49:7, the suffering servant is "an abomination to the people," rejected and despised; in Job 19:19, Job's friends "abhor him" and turn away from him.
H8581.origine: The Hebrew verb תעב (tʿb) expresses visceral disgust and moral rejection. It is related to the idea of what raises the stomach, what is repugnant. The word טעם (taʿam, taste) shares the same root: what one abhors, one cannot "taste." Derivatives include תוֹעֵבָה (toʿéva), the abomination itself. This verb belongs to a rich semantic field in biblical Hebrew to express moral and religious rejection.
H8581.emploi: This verb appears about 20 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom books (Psalms, Job), the Law (Deuteronomy), and the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel). It describes religious disgust: idolatrous practices, acts contrary to the Law are "abominable" in the eyes of God. It also expresses social rejection: Job's friends abhorred him, the people abhorred the Servant of Isaiah. Sometimes disgust is physical: in Psalms 107:18, the sick "abhorred" food at the brink of death. The word thus oscillates between moral religious condemnation and visceral or relational repugnance.
H8581.portee: This verb reminds us that biblical faith is not limited to cold obedience: it engages emotions, the heart. To abhor evil is to deeply reject it, with our whole being, not just out of duty. For the believer, this invites scrutiny of what one truly abhors — the real idols, hidden compromises — and to cultivate a proper repulsion towards what offends God, while maintaining compassion for those who stray.

sens: To wander physically, to get lost on the way
To stagger, to lose balance or stability (in a physical sense or due to intoxication)
To stray morally, to turn away from good and justice
To be deceived, led astray
To cause someone to stray, to seduce or deceive them
To deviate from the right path, to stray from the straight way
H8582.detail:
1. To wander physically or roam: the verb describes one who gets lost, who goes back and forth without direction (Genesis 37:15 — Joseph in the fields is looking for his brothers and a man asks him: "What are you seeking? I heard them say: Let us go to Dothan."). It is the image of a person who does not know where to go.
2. To stagger or destabilize, particularly under the influence of intoxication: Job 12:25 describes those who "stumble in darkness" and "wander like drunken men," unable to walk straight. The word then evokes a loss of balance and self-control.
3. To stray morally or spiritually, to turn away from what is right and good: in Isaiah 3:12, corrupt leaders "lead astray" the people by guiding them poorly. It is to intentionally or unintentionally deviate from God's path and His commandments.
4. To be deceived or seduced by false words: in Jeremiah 23:32, false prophets "lead astray" the people with their lies. The heart can no longer discern truth from falsehood.
5. To cause someone to stray, to intentionally deceive or seduce them: one who "leads astray" is a cunning leader or seducer who diverts others from truth or good. In Isaiah 9:15, the prophets and elders "lead astray" by deceiving the people about the true way.
6. To stray from the straight path, to go on the paths of perdition: Psalms 119:176 expresses this idea: "I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant," for the soul strays from God's flock and His ordinances.
H8582.origine: The Hebrew verb תָּעָה comes from a primitive root that fundamentally means "to wander" or "to roam." The starting image is that of aimless movement, of uncertain steps or lost direction. This root also appears in related nouns describing wandering or straying. The word can have a physical connotation (getting lost on the way) or moral and spiritual (deviating from the right path). It is a very vivid verb in the Bible to express separation from God and His ways.
H8582.emploi: The verb appears about 45 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. It first describes physical wandering: Abraham says that God made him "wander" far from his home (Genesis 20:13), Hagar and Ishmael wander in the desert (Genesis 21:14). Very often, the word takes on a moral or spiritual value: the people "stray" by following idols or false prophets, or spiritual leaders "lead astray" intentionally the flock entrusted to their care (Jeremiah 50:6: the shepherds "led them astray, made them wander through the mountains"). The Psalms use it to express the risk of straying from God's commandments (Psalms 119:110: "I do not stray far from your ordinances"). Intoxication can also cause this "straying" (Job 12:25). The word can finally mean "to deceive" or "to seduce" in the sense of leading someone intentionally away from the truth.
H8582.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that there is a path to follow — that of God — and a real risk of straying from it, either through ignorance and weakness or through seduction and lies. The Bible uses the image of straying to show that a life without God is a life without direction, groping and lost. It also invites vigilance against those who might "lead us astray": false shepherds or false words. Finally, it assures that God seeks the lost sheep, as in Psalms 119:176.

sens: King of Hamath during the time of David
Ally of David against Hadadezer
H8583.detail: Toi is a Syrian king who reigns over the city of Hamath at the time when David conquers the Near East. When he learns that David has defeated Hadadezer, his own enemy, Toi sends his son Joram (called Hadoram in Chronicles) to David with gifts to congratulate and greet him — a common diplomatic practice among kings. Through this gesture, Toi acknowledges David's power and seeks to establish an alliance with him.
H8583.origine: The name Toi literally means "one who wanders" or "who moves," a poetic image. This king bore this name in the history of the ancient East, and Hebrew scribes transmitted it as such in the royal accounts.
H8583.emploi: Toi appears only four times in the Bible: twice in 2 Samuel 8 (verses 9 and 10) and twice in 1 Chronicles 18 (verses 9 and 10), which report the same event. The account in Chronicles calls him Thohu, while Samuel names him Toi; these two forms refer to the same person. His intervention is brief but revealing: it shows how neighboring kings reacted to David's rise to power and how they sought his friendship.
H8583.portee: The account of Toi illustrates how David's power and justice earned him the respect of other nations. For the Christian reader, this episode reminds us that victory according to God attracts not only opponents but also allies, and that it bears witness to God's purpose among the peoples.

sens: Material proof or act that establishes the truth of a fact
Word of God, divine revelation that attests to His will
Inscription or sacred ordinance that confirms and seals the Word of God
H8584.detail:
1. The testimony is primarily a concrete proof that is exhibited to confirm an agreement or transaction. In Ruth 4:7, the act of removing the sandal and giving it to the other party served as material testimony, a visible proof that made the transaction legal and irrevocable before witnesses: it was the living document of the contract.
2. The testimony also refers to the prophetic word of God, what He reveals and commands. In Isaiah 8:16, the prophet must wrap and seal the oracle (the divine word) as something precious given to the disciples: the testimony is the solemn transmission of divine will.
3. More broadly, the testimony is the revelation of God shaped, established, capable of guiding the people. In Isaiah 8:20, "the law and the testimony" together are the unchanging standard by which all preaching must be evaluated: without them, the people will have no dawn, no salvation, nor light.
H8584.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to repeat, to testify, to attest." It is related to the common word for "witness." The initial image is that of a solemn repetition in the presence of witnesses: one reaffirms, one certifies. The term thus evokes the idea of successive confirmations, of words that accumulate to establish absolute certainty.
H8584.emploi: The word appears 3 times in the Segond. It is first used in a material and legal sense in Ruth 4:7, where it refers to the rite that seals a redemption contract. It then takes on a prophetic and religious sense in Isaiah 8:16 and 8:20, where it designates the revealed word of God, either as an oracle to be sealed and transmitted, or as a teaching norm that saves the people. In these last two usages, the testimony is what endures, what remains unchanging, and what confirms the truth.
H8584.portee: For the believer, the word reminds us that the revelation of God is neither vague nor subjective: it is a solid testimony, attested and sealed words, that can be grasped and transmitted. This encourages trust in the Word of God as an established proof, and to know it so as not to be led astray by false teachings.

sens: Trench dug in the ground to allow water to pass
Conduit or channel built to bring water from one place to another
Furrow or passage carved by the natural flow of water
H8585A.detail:
1. The ditch is primarily a practical trench dug in the ground: at the time of the sacrifice on Mount Carmel, Elijah "made a ditch around the altar, large enough to hold two measures of seed" (1 Kings 18:32), and "the water flowed around the altar, and they filled the ditch with water" (1 Kings 18:35) to better demonstrate the miracle of fire falling from heaven. It is a hollow intended to collect or allow water to circulate.
2. The word also designates an engineering work to channel water: Hezekiah "made the pool and the aqueduct, and brought the waters into the city" (2 Kings 20:20), that is, a water supply system, and the Bible mentions "the aqueduct of the upper pool" (2 Kings 18:17), a public infrastructure that the Assyrians used as a landmark.
3. The word also applies to natural paths carved by water: God asks Job, "Who has opened a passage for the rain, and traced the way for the thunder and lightning" (Job 38:25), where the ditch is the furrow that water shapes in nature through its flow.
H8585A.origine: The Hebrew word תְּעָלָה (te'alah) comes from a root meaning "to dig" or "to bore." It evokes the image of a trench or canal cut into the earth — a practical and visible work. The word appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in contexts of hydraulic engineering (the kings of Israel and Judah built aqueducts) and in descriptions of natural phenomena (water carves its path).
H8585A.emploi: This word appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible. The first three usages recount the story of Elijah's sacrifice on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:32, 35, 38): Elijah digs a ditch around the altar to pour water into it, thus reinforcing the miraculous nature of the divine fire that will consume everything, including the water. The next two usages refer to the hydraulic works of King Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:17 and 20:20): a famous aqueduct supplies Jerusalem with drinking water, a defense against sieges. The usage in Job 38:25 extends the meaning to the cosmic and natural level: the "ditches" or paths carved by rain and lightning in the atmosphere show God's creative power. The word thus moves from the concrete (a ditch cut by hand) to the abstract (the paths of water in nature).
H8585A.portee: This word reminds readers how God provides for the needs of men, first through the practical achievements of human labor (the aqueducts), and then through His sovereign action on creation (rain, lightning). The ditch of Elijah's sacrifice also symbolizes honesty and the absence of deception: the water generously poured into the ditch shows that the miracle is not a trick. For the Christian reader, it is an image of God's role as provider and master of creation.

sens: Action of healing, closing a wound
Restoration of bodily health
Remedy, medical treatment
Moral or spiritual restoration
H8585B.detail: 1. The word first designates the natural process of healing: the formation of new flesh and skin that closes a wound (this is the most concrete sense). In Jeremiah 30:13, God tells the people that no one "binds your wound" — no one can stop the bleeding or facilitate this healing. 2. More broadly, it refers to the complete restoration of health: the return to the normal state of the body after an illness or injury. In Jeremiah 46:11, Egypt seeks remedies to heal, but "there is no healing" — no treatment can save her. 3. The word can also refer to the remedy itself, the concrete means of healing: balm, bandage, medication. 4. In a broader sense, it can extend to spiritual or moral healing: the restoration of a nation wounded by sin, punishment, or defeat.
H8585B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root (עלה) that essentially means "to rise" or "to go up." The initial image is that of flesh that "rises" or reforms above a wound. This root appears in other Hebrew words related to restoration and uplift. The Greek of the Septuagint translates this word with terms close to "therapy" or "medical healing."
H8585B.emploi: This word is infrequent in the Hebrew Bible (two occurrences in known usages). It appears in two passages from the prophet Jeremiah, both in a context of divine judgment. In Jeremiah 30:13, the prophet reproaches Jerusalem that no one can heal her wounds: it is the image of an incurable injury, reflecting the abandonment of the people. In Jeremiah 46:11, Egypt seeks in vain for balms from Gilead to heal herself: here too, healing remains impossible. In these two passages, the word signifies not only the process of healing but also the hope of restoration that remains unattainable. The word thus emphasizes medical impotence and, by extension, political and spiritual impotence in the face of God's judgment.
H8585B.portee: This word reminds the believer that certain wounds — particularly those inflicted by divine judgment — can only be healed by the grace of God alone. It invites seeking healing not in human remedies, however prestigious they may be (the balm of Gilead was renowned), but in the mercy and intervention of the Lord. For God's people, it is also a hidden promise: if healing seems impossible, God alone can make it possible (see Jeremiah 30:17, where God promises to heal).

sens: Light, fanciful behavior, lacking maturity
Action or word that causes disorder and misfortune
Mockery, derision from one who takes pleasure in the misfortune of others
H8586.detail: 1. The word primarily designates a light and childish behavior, devoid of wisdom: it is to act like a child, without considering the consequences. In Isaiah 3:4, God threatens Judah by giving them young leaders, children who will govern — that is, light and whimsical beings, incapable of leading the people. 2. From there, the word takes on the meaning of calamity or misfortune, but a misfortune that comes from this lightness, from these irresponsible acts. It is also what provokes ruin and turmoil. 3. Finally, it can evoke wicked satisfaction in the misfortune of others: in Isaiah 66:4, the Lord says He will take pleasure in the misfortune of those who have rejected Him, as a form of divine vengeance or mockery.
H8586.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of playing, of aimless amusement, of mocking. Originally, it is the image of childish and futile play — from which naturally arises the idea of what is vain, devoid of meaning, and ultimately destructive. The root expresses carelessness and a lack of moral weight.
H8586.emploi: The word appears twice in the Tanakh, only in the book of Isaiah. In both contexts, it refers to predictions of misfortune addressed to a people who have disobeyed God. In Isaiah 3:4, God punishes Judah by sending them childish and whimsical rulers — an image of political chaos. In Isaiah 66:4, the Lord expresses His readiness to take pleasure in the misfortune of those who reject Him, seeing it as a form of divine retribution. In both cases, the word underscores both the absurdity and the gravity of judgment.
H8586.portee: This word reminds us that abandoning wisdom and obedience to God produces chaos and misfortune, often embodied in social and political disorder. It invites the reader to recognize that childish and irresponsible acts have real consequences, and that God, in His justice, allows rebels to taste the bitter fruits of their lightness and rebellion.

sens: What is hidden, concealed, not seen or unknown
What is kept silent, not revealed to others
The secret thoughts and intentions of the heart, hidden from all eyes
What is mysterious, unfathomable, difficult to understand
H8587.detail: 1. The word primarily designates what is hidden, concealed, distant from sight — something removed and invisible. In Job 28:11, it evokes underground waters and buried treasures that God "brings to light": it is the image of something hidden deep that is brought to the surface. 2. The secret is also what is not said, what is kept to oneself. In Job 11:6, God possesses the "secrets of His wisdom": there are things of God so profound that even the wise can only know them if God reveals them. 3. The word particularly applies to the secrets of the heart — the intimate thoughts, desires, and intentions of each person. In Psalms 44:22, God "knows the secrets of the heart": nothing that happens inside us escapes His gaze. 4. These secrets are often what cannot be fathomed, which exceeds our understanding: we think of God's mysterious wisdom, His hidden plans that He reveals to us gradually.
H8587.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of "closing," of "tightening" — what cannot be easily opened, what remains closed. This root aligns with the image of the secret as something closed and guarded. The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, underscoring its particular and grave nature: it designates not a trivial secret, but what is authentically hidden or unfathomable.
H8587.emploi: This word appears three times, all in the wisdom literature (Job and Psalms), where it almost always concerns the secrets of God. In Job 11:6, the wise man Zophar makes it clear to Job that God possesses secrets of wisdom far beyond what Job can grasp — it is an invitation to humility. In Job 28:11, the passage speaks of secrets hidden in the earth, which broadens the image: it is the invisible, underground world that God controls. In Psalms 44:22, the emphasis is on divine knowledge: God knows the secrets of the human heart, our most hidden thoughts. Everywhere, the secret is linked to what escapes ordinary man and pertains to the knowledge or power of God.
H8587.portee: This word invites the believer to the awareness that nothing is hidden from God, that every secret thought of the heart is known to Him — which calls us to honesty and sincerity before God. It also teaches us humility: there are secrets of God, depths of His wisdom and His plans that we cannot fathom, except through the revelation He graciously grants us.

sens: Luxury, refinement, that which provides pleasure and enjoyment
Object or person dear, precious, beloved
Sweetness, charm, grace
H8588.detail: 1. The word primarily designates luxury, the refined and delicate pleasures sought by wealthy people: it is the idea of living in abundance and sensuality. Ecclesiastes 2:8 gives the most vivid image: the wise man enumerates his accumulated riches and pleasures, including "the delights of the sons of man," that is, the sensual entertainments that a powerful man can afford. 2. The word also applies to what one cherishes, what one loves tenderly — a person, a place, a possession that is precious to us. Micah 1:16 and 2:9 show this by speaking of the "cherished" children and houses of the people, from which they will be torn away: it is what one loses with pain. 3. In poetry, the word can simply evoke beauty, charm, grace: Song of Solomon 7:7 applies "delight" to the beloved, to express all her allure and tenderness.
H8588.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of delighting, tasting with pleasure. It primarily designates sensory pleasure — the sweetness of a flavor, the enjoyment of a good — and then, by extension, everything that pleases, charms, or rejoices. It is a word that paints the pleasant and lovable in all its forms.
H8588.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the wisdom books and poetry. Proverbs 19:10 uses it to criticize the fool who lives luxuriously without having the rank: delight here is a sign of social incongruity. Ecclesiastes 2:8 uses it to describe the pleasures accumulated by the wise experimenter — but in a context of vanity, since all this proves to be futile. Song of Solomon 7:7 makes it a tender and loving word, characterizing the grace of the beloved. Micah 1:16 and 2:9 give it a tone of mourning: the delights one enjoyed will disappear, and it is a catastrophe. The word thus shifts between the critique of luxury, the nostalgia for lost pleasure, and the expression of affection.
H8588.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on the role of enjoyment and pleasure in their life. The Bible does not condemn pleasure in itself, but warns against luxury that separates from God and against attachment to material goods: Proverbs 19:10 reminds us that prosperity only makes sense if it is grounded in wisdom. For the Christian, the word also says that true delight — true enjoyment — resides in God alone, not in perishable things.

sens: voluntary abstinence from food
humiliation of oneself through deprivation
religious practice of asceticism and penance
H8589.detail:
1. Fasting is the abstention from food for a specified period. It is a voluntary act that the one fasting freely chooses for a time. In Ezra 9:5, Ezra rises "from the midst of his humiliation": this expression describes the state of lowering in which fasting has placed him, sitting on the ground in mourning and contrition.

2. Fasting is also a humiliation of oneself: by renouncing nourishment, one weakens their body and thereby shows that they are giving up their comforts and submitting. It is a gesture that cries out to God: "I am unworthy, I disavow myself, I seek your forgiveness."

3. It is a common religious practice among believers in the Old Testament, often associated with intense prayer, mourning, or repentance. It accompanies intercession: fasting tells God, "I am truly serious; what I am asking is dear to my heart."
H8589.origine: The Hebrew word תַּעֲנִית (ta'anit) comes from a root that expresses the idea of affliction and deprivation. It is a practice deeply rooted in Jewish piety: fasting is one of the most visible and embodied forms of humility before God. The root refers to the image of a weakened body, an empty stomach, crying out to heaven.
H8589.emploi: This word appears only once in Ezra 9:5, at a crucial moment: Ezra has learned that the Israelites returned from exile have mingled with foreign peoples in violation of the Law. Dismayed, he fasts and prays to intercede for the people and seek God's forgiveness. The context shows that fasting is not a light personal penance, but a total expression of spiritual pain and intercessory commitment. It is a crisis fast, a national repentance, accompanying pleading prayer.
H8589.portee: For today's reader, fasting reminds us that true humility before God is not limited to words: it is embodied in the body, in concrete renunciation. Fasting is saying no to one's instincts and comforts to say yes to God. Ezra shows that fasting is never an end in itself, a spiritual achievement, but a means of approaching God with all one's afflicted being and interceding for others.

sens: City in western Galilee, in ancient Israel
Canaanite city in the territory of Issachar, assigned to the tribe of Manasseh
H8590.detail: Taanach was a fortified city in Canaan, conquered by Joshua during Israel's invasion (Joshua 12:21). Although located in the territory of Issachar, it was given to the tribe of Manasseh, and even ceded to the Levites of the Kohathite family (Joshua 21:25). Its name means "sandy," which reflects the terrain of the Galilean region. It is often mentioned alongside Megiddo, another important fortress of the time. It experiences a memorable episode during the battle where Deborah and Barak confront the army of Sisera: it is near Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo, that the kings of Canaan are defeated without being able to gather plunder (Judges 5:19).
H8590.origine: The name Taanach, whose variant Tanach literally means "sandy," describes the type of terrain in this region. It was also known as Aner (Joshua 21:25), indicating that this place had multiple names. Taanach was a typical Canaanite fortified city, well-positioned on the trade routes of Galilee.
H8590.emploi: Taanach appears seven times in the Bible, primarily in the account of the conquest and division of the lands. It is first listed among the Canaanite cities defeated by Joshua (Joshua 12:21), then among those assigned to Manasseh despite their location in the territory of Issachar (Joshua 17:11). It becomes a Levitical city (Joshua 21:25). However, the Manassites were unable to drive out the Canaanite inhabitants (Judges 1:27), and it thus remained a Canaanite enclave in Israelite territory. Taanach is also the site of a memorable victory against the Canaanite kings (Judges 5:19), and it remains an important administrative center during the monarchy (1 Kings 4:12).

sens: To make fun of someone, to ridicule
To deceive, to mislead through mockery
To treat with contempt and derision
H8591.detail: 1. To mock is to openly make fun of someone, to turn them into a subject of ridicule. It is a mockery that seeks to humiliate. In Genesis 27:12, Jacob fears that his father Isaac, upon touching him, will discover the deception and call him a "liar"—that is, someone who does not deserve trust, who abuses through deceitful words. 2. The word can also refer to one who deceives through their words, leading others astray. Mockery and lying go hand in hand: one mocks someone by deceiving them. 3. In 2 Chronicles 36:16, the Israelites "mocked" the prophets of God—they despised them, ridiculed them, refusing to take them seriously. It is an active contempt, a mockery that rejects divine warning.
H8591.origine: The Hebrew word תָּעַע comes from a root that evokes the idea of deceiving and mocking. The structure of the verb (Pilpel) intensifies the meaning: it is a resolute, persistent mockery. The same word can describe one who lies or mocks, as both abuse words to deceive or humiliate.
H8591.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 27:12, Jacob fears being discovered as a "liar"—someone who abuses his father's trust through cunning and deceit. In 2 Chronicles 36:16, it describes how Israel mocked the prophets, despising them and refusing to listen. Both usages intertwine deception and mockery: to mock is to deceive through contempt, refusing to take seriously.
H8591.portee: To mock God or His messengers is to commit a grave act: it is both to despise and to deceive, refusing to receive His warning. The text from Chronicles shows how this prolonged mockery brings about divine judgment "without remedy." For the believer, mocking the Word of God is the opposite of wisdom: it is to choose voluntary blindness.

sens: Strength, ability to accomplish great acts
Authority, domination exercised by the powerful
Divine glory and majesty manifested through works
H8592.detail:
1. The word denotes physical or moral strength capable of accomplishing great things: it is the power to act, to achieve. In Psalms 68:36, God gives His people strength and power, equipping them with the means to stand firm and overcome.
2. This word also evokes authority and domination: one who possesses power has the ability to command, to direct events. It is a force that is exercised.
3. When applied to God, the term expresses His incomparable majesty and glory manifested in His powerful acts: divine power is revealed when God intervenes in the history of His people.
H8592.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of strength and solidity. It belongs to the family of words speaking of strength, vigor, and effectiveness. The psalmist, in speaking of God's power, emphasizes that what makes the Lord fearsome (terrible, worthy of reverence) is precisely this irresistible power: He can accomplish all that He wills.
H8592.emploi: The word appears once in the Bible, in Psalms 68:36, in a context of praise. After inviting to contemplate the power of God manifested in His sanctuary, the psalmist proclaims that it is the God of Israel who gives His people strength and power. It is a power acknowledged as a divine gift: it is not a strength that the people possess on their own, but a power that God imparts. The liturgical context suggests that this power is exercised in the realm of spiritual liberation and victory.
H8592.portee: This word reminds the believer that true power comes from God alone: it does not reside in money, technology, or political influence, but in the strength that God grants to His people. It is an invitation to recognize that our victory over evil, our ability to stand firm in faith, and our effectiveness in serving God depend entirely on this power He entrusts to us.

sens: Cutting instrument used for shaving the beard or hair
Sheath or casing that envelops a blade
Blade or knife used for cutting
That which cuts, wounds, or judges harshly
H8593.detail:
1. The razor is the actual shaving instrument. A Nazarite must not shave: he is forbidden to allow a razor to pass over his head for the entire duration of his vow (Numbers 6:5). Ezekiel is commanded to take a barber's razor to shave his head and beard as a sign of mourning and destruction (Ezekiel 5:1).
2. A sheath or casing that protects the blade of a sword or knife. When David takes Goliath's sword, he draws it from its sheath before beheading the Philistine (1 Samuel 17:51). The sword of God must come out of its sheath to execute His judgment on all flesh (Ezekiel 21:9).
3. A smaller cutting instrument, such as a penknife or knife: the king's secretary uses his penknife to cut the scroll of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 36:23).
4. Figuratively, the tongue of the wicked becomes a weapon that cuts and wounds like a sharp razor (Psalms 52:4). It invents malice with destructive precision and effectiveness. The sword of God is also compared to this instrument that cuts, judges, and slices mercilessly.
H8593.origine: The Hebrew word ta'ar primarily refers to a cutting instrument. Its primitive image is that of something that strips away, that removes: the razor removes hair, the sheath envelops and protects before the blade is drawn. This image of sharpness and nakedness is found in all uses of the term. The word is primarily attested in contexts of Nazarite vows (Levitical law), battle, and divine judgment, where the notion of loss, destruction, or exposure is central.
H8593.emploi: The word appears thirteen times in the Hebrew Bible. Five occurrences concern the razor in the strict sense: the vow of the Nazarite who does not shave, or Ezekiel who must shave as a sign of judgment. Seven occurrences refer to the sheath of the sword or knife, particularly during battles or when God draws His sword to judge. One occurrence (Jeremiah 36:23) uses it for a small cutting instrument. Figuratively (Psalms 52:4), the tongue of the wicked is a sharp razor. These uses show that the word glides from the concrete (the tool) to the abstract (everything that cuts, destroys, or exposes).
H8593.portee: The razor in the Bible reminds us that vows and outward signs engage our entire life toward God. The blade that cuts and the tongue that wounds show that our words can destroy or build up: they are never neutral. The sword of God that comes out of its sheath invites us to respect His fearsome justice and to fear Him who alone can judge.

sens: person taken and held as a guarantee of an agreement or ransom
living security given to ensure the fulfillment of a promise
pledge of safety between two parties
H8594.detail:
1. A person taken by a conqueror to guarantee that the defeated party will fulfill their commitments or pay what they owe. When the king of Israel Joash attacked Jerusalem and defeated the king of Judah Amaziah, he took "hostages" along with the gold and silver from the temple: these individuals remained captive and would only be released if Judah met the imposed conditions (2 Kings 14:14).
2. A form of security between two kingdoms: by handing over important individuals (often members of the royal family), the defeated party proved their intention to honor the treaty, as they risked their lives. It is an exchange of values — material goods and lives for a promise made.
H8594.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to mix" or "to guarantee." The hostage embodies the intertwining of the two parties and their interests: their person is the living link that guarantees the fulfillment of the agreement. In ancient Hebrew, this term also refers to a pledge or a guarantee — anything or anyone given to ensure the execution of an obligation.
H8594.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, in parallel passages of the same event: 2 Kings 14:14 and 2 Chronicles 25:24. Both verses recount how Joash, king of Israel, after his military victory over Amaziah, king of Judah, took hostages from Jerusalem. They are among the spoils of war — gold, silver, temple vessels — and mark the political subjugation of one kingdom to another. The term thus designates a diplomatic and military practice of the ancient Near East.
H8594.portee: This word reminds us that in human conflicts, even innocent people become pawns of power. For the Christian reader, it illustrates how power dynamics dominate relationships between kingdoms when God is not acknowledged. It is also a lesson on the price of sin and rebellion: Judah, having turned away from the Lord, suffers defeat and sees its inhabitants become hostages.

sens: Error, misleading illusion
False work, vain and unfounded effort
Mockery, derision
H8595.detail:
1. Error or misleading illusion: that which misleads the mind and causes it to believe something false. It is the opposite of solid and lasting truth.
2. False work, vain and unfounded effort: a creation that has no real value, no true substance. In Jeremiah 10:15 and 51:18, idols are described as a "work of deception" — they are nothing but empty vanity, nothingness shaped into wood or stone.
3. Mockery or derision: the underlying idea of a false appearance that mocks those who trust in it, covering them with ridicule and shame.
H8595.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes shaking, wavering, instability. A deception shakes, stirs, causes one to lose footing: it is the opposite of what is firm and true. The nuance of "mockery" also relates to the fact that the deceived becomes an object of ridicule.
H8595.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in Jeremiah (10:15 and 51:18), in the same oracle against idols. Jeremiah reproaches idolaters for making gods that are nothing but deception and vanity — human works without life, power, or truth. The context is one of radical condemnation of idolatry: these idols, conceived as deception, will perish on the day of judgment.
H8595.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that everything not founded on God and His truth is empty illusion. Jeremiah warns us that false religion — one built on lies or human productions — leads to ruin. It is a call to discern between the true and the false, between what endures and what collapses.

sens: Percussion instrument consisting of a membrane stretched over a frame, often adorned with jingles or bells
Portable instrument used especially by women for dance and celebration
Symbol of joy, rejoicing, and festivity in a cultic or popular context
Figure of gaiety that disappears when judgment or mourning arrives
H8596.detail:
1. The tambourine is a simple yet resonant instrument: a round or square frame over which a skin is stretched, and adorned with small jingles that produce a sharp and joyful sound when struck or shaken. David and all Israel played it before God while dancing (1 Chronicles 13:8), which shows its common cultic use.
2. The women of Israel primarily used it to dance and celebrate victories or family joys. When David returned after killing the Philistine, the women came out to meet him with tambourines (1 Samuel 18:6). Jephthah's daughter came out to meet her father with tambourines and dances (Judges 11:34), a traditional mark of honor and joy.
3. The tambourine is inseparable from festivity and praise. The psalmist calls to praise God "with the tambourine and with dances" (Psalms 150:4), and it was played during celebrations (Genesis 31:27): it is the instrument of joyful celebration.
4. Conversely, the prophet Isaiah denounces those who think only of feasts and music without fearing God, and announces that the tambourine will cease, that joy will disappear before judgment (Isaiah 5:12; 24:8). The silence of the tambourine symbolizes mourning and the absence of blessing.
H8596.origine: The Hebrew word תֹּף (toph) designates this particular instrument since ancient Near Eastern times. Its etymology is uncertain, but its meaning is stable throughout the Bible: it is a concrete object and a social reality well rooted in feasts and celebrations. The tambourine appears in contexts of personal rejoicing (family celebrations, victories) and cultic (praise to God), always associated with dance and song.
H8596.emploi: The tambourine is mentioned seventeen times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the Psalms and historical books. It first appears as an instrument of victory and festivity: Miriam and the women play the tambourine after the crossing of the Red Sea (mentioned in the references), and the women play it to welcome David (1 Samuel 18:6). It is also an instrument of worship: David plays it before the ark (1 Chronicles 13:8), and the Psalms call for it as a means to praise God (Psalms 81:3; 150:4). But the prophet Isaiah mentions it ironically or negatively: those who feast without fearing God play the tambourine (Isaiah 5:12), and judgment will render the tambourine mute (Isaiah 24:8). This contrast shows that the instrument is only good if it expresses true pious joy, not ungodly frivolity.
H8596.portee: The tambourine reminds us that joy is a legitimate part of the Christian faith. It is an instrument of praise, not of worldly distraction: when played to celebrate God's victory or beauty, it is a pious act. But it also teaches that joy without God, a celebration without respect for His word, leads to silence and mourning. For the believer, the tambourine invites us to rejoice in God with all our heart, not just for fleeting pleasures.

sens: Brilliant beauty, visible splendor of a person or thing
Adornment, precious ornament that enhances appearance
Honor, renown, recognized dignity of a person or people
Radiance, shining manifestation of divine power or majesty
H8597.detail:
1. The word first denotes striking, impressive beauty. When Isaiah speaks of Ephraim as "the fading flower, which makes the splendor of its adornment" (Isaiah 28:1), he evokes this visible splendor that attracts the gaze and inspires admiration.
2. It also refers to the clothing and jewelry that adorn and magnify a person — visible wealth on a body. Aaron wears "sacred garments, to mark his dignity and serve as his adornment" (Exodus 28:2): these garments do not just clothe him, they adorn and elevate him.
3. The word takes on a moral and social meaning: honor, renown, what makes the reputation of a person or people. A wise person "makes his glory to forget offenses" (Proverbs 19:11) — he finds his honor in self-control, not in vengeance.
4. Finally, glory becomes the radiance of divine power, the glorious manifestation of God Himself. Jeremiah speaks of the city as "a subject of joy, praise, and glory" among the nations (Jeremiah 33:9), for it will testify to the goodness and greatness of the Lord.
H8597.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "weight," of "heaviness" — not in a negative sense, but in the sense of what has weight, importance, gravity. A weighty thing is something that matters, that impresses. This root is related to the notion of "majestic heaviness." In Greek, the word "doxa" (δόξα) translates it, bringing the idea of renown and positive judgment. Biblical glory is what weighs, what matters, what is seen and imposes itself.
H8597.emploi: This word appears about fifty times in the Old Testament, especially in poetic and prophetic passages. It first denotes material adornments — sacred garments, jewelry (Exodus 28:2, Ezekiel 16:12). It then expands to the splendor of kingdoms and the renown of kings (Esther 1:4, Jeremiah 48:17). An important dimension is the glory of Israel or Jerusalem, a symbol of divine blessing (Jeremiah 13:11, Isaiah 62:3). Gradually, the word rises toward the divine: glory becomes God's own attribute, His visible majesty (1 Chronicles 29:11, Psalms 96:6), that fills the temple and fills the universe. The meaning also nuances towards individual pride — a misplaced glory, the one one gives oneself (Proverbs 19:11).
H8597.portee: This word invites the believer to see beauty and honor not as ends in themselves, but as reflections of divine glory. When Isaiah calls Jerusalem to "put on your garments of glory" (Isaiah 52:1), he is not speaking of vanity, but of a people adorned with justice and God's blessing. Meditating on biblical glory teaches that true honor comes from God, that the deepest beauty is that which manifests His power, and that our own dignity depends on our relationship with Him.

sens: Round and sweet fruit of the apple tree, golden or red in color
Fruit tree that produces apples
Image of sweetness, fragrance, and beauty in love and tenderness
Natural wealth and sign of life in creation
H8598.detail: 1. The apple is primarily the fruit of the apple tree, tasty and fragrant: in Song of Solomon 2:5, the beloved asks for apples to be comforted, and in Song of Solomon 7:9, the fragrance of apples is compared to the breath of the beloved, so sweet and alluring it is. 2. The apple tree is the tree itself, appreciated for the shade it provides: in Song of Solomon 2:3, the beloved desires to sit under its shade, as it is a pleasant refuge in the midst of the forest. 3. The apple becomes a poetic image of what is beautiful and precious: in Proverbs 25:11, a word spoken at the right moment shines like apples of gold in settings of silver, meaning its beauty comes from the harmony between the right word and the opportune moment. 4. The apple tree also represents life and the fertility of the land: in Joel 1:12, when drought withers it along with other trees, it is a sign that joy has left men, for creation itself languishes.
H8598.origine: The Hebrew word תַּפּוּחַ comes from a root that evokes the idea of something sweet and comforting. The apple tree was cultivated in the Holy Land and in the ancient Near East, and its sweet, rare, and precious fruits were part of the delights of the Mediterranean world. The golden apple of the Bible also evokes ancient mythologies where the golden fruit symbolizes wealth and desire.
H8598.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the lyrical poetry of the Song of Solomon, where it adorns the language of love. In Proverbs 25:11, the golden apple illustrates the beauty of a well-placed word. In Song of Solomon 2:3 and 2:5, it expresses the sweetness of the beloved and the comfort sought from him. In Song of Solomon 7:9 and 8:5, it appears again in poetic and nostalgic descriptions. In Joel 1:12, it becomes a symbol of rural life and the prosperity that calamity destroys. The context changes: sacred in Proverbs, romantic in the Song, prophetic in Joel, but it always carries a sense of preciousness and warmth.
H8598.portee: The apple reminds us that God has given fruits to the earth for our joy and comfort. In biblical poetry, it teaches that true riches are not gold or silver, but a wise word at the right moment (Proverbs), tender love and sharing (Song), and the simple life that we can lose if we turn away from God (Joel). For the believer, it invites us to appreciate the concrete gifts of God and the beauty of His creations.

sens: Descendant of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
H8599A.detail: 1. Thappuach is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. He is the son of Hebron and the brother of Kore, Rekem, and Shema. His name simply appears in the list of descendants of Caleb, without any particular narrative.
H8599A.origine: The name Thappuach literally means "the city of the apple" or refers to the apple, a fruit known in Israel. It is a Hebrew proper name whose root evokes a fruit or a place. There is also a city in Israel called Thappuach (in the region of Ephraim and northern Judah), but this character bears the same name as a personal identifier.
H8599A.emploi: Thappuach appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:43, in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Judah and the family of Caleb. He is listed among the sons of Hebron without any events of his life being reported. This type of genealogical mention was important for establishing heritage and kinship within the large families of the tribe.

sens: City in the territory of Ephraim, on the border with Manasseh
H8599B.detail: 1. Tappuach is a city located in the southern part of the region that Ephraim received as an inheritance after the conquest of Canaan. Its name means "the city of the apple" or "the city of the apple tree" in Hebrew. It was situated on the border between Ephraim and Manasseh, which explains why it is sometimes mentioned as a possession of both tribes: the territory belonged to the sons of Manasseh, but the border point of Tappuach belonged to the sons of Ephraim (Joshua 17:8). It was among the royal Canaanite cities conquered by Joshua (Joshua 12:17).
H8599B.origine: The Hebrew name תַּפּוּחַ (tappuach) comes from the root that designates the apple or the apple tree. It reflects the importance of this fruit cultivation in that area, a common practice in the fertile regions of Canaan. The name describes the identity and resources of this border city.
H8599B.emploi: Tappuach is mentioned three times in the Old Testament, all in the book of Joshua at the time of the division of the promised land. It first appears as a royal Canaanite city conquered (Joshua 12:17), then in the description of the borders of the territory of Ephraim (Joshua 16:8), and finally during the delimitation of the lands between Ephraim and Manasseh (Joshua 17:8). These three references show its status as a strategic border point whose possession was shared between two tribes.

sens: City in Judah
H8599G.detail: Tappuach is a city located in the hilly region of southern Judah during the time of the conquest of the territory by Israel. Its name literally means "the city of the apple" or "the city of the apple tree" in Hebrew, suggesting that this place was known for its apple orchards or fruits. It is listed among the cities belonging to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:34).
H8599G.origine: The name Tappuach comes from the Hebrew root tap.pu.ach, which designates the apple tree or the apple. This etymology reflects the agricultural environment and characteristic vegetation of the site. The suffix -ah in Hebrew often indicates a place or region, thus transforming the name of the fruit into a city name.
H8599G.emploi: Tappuach appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the book of Joshua chapter 15, where the cities assigned to the tribe of Judah are enumerated. It is mentioned among the localities of the hill country or the "lowland" (shephelah) of Judah. This unique mention indicates that it was a minor but recognized city in the biblical territorial lists. Its presence in this legal document suggests an administrative status in the territorial organization of Israel.
